per_item.reference: Before construction: determine the slopes with a water level; draw the plan from them; mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare. Construction: raise the bunds to profile, main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30; water them as they are built so that they compact. Openings: leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. Organisation: the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation. Site: replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site.

history.content: Set out the construction procedure.

draws.answer: Cut the trees to about 2 m high, and cut those trees down to the ground. Then rebuild the lowland with a water level grid, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. Draw the plan from the slopes you measured with a water level. Mark the plan with pegs at 5 to 10 m intervals. Build the main bund at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high; secondary ones at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. Water them as you build so they compact. Leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund. For a plan drawn from your own observations, see ICAT.

From the 2008 commercial reference, the building: the houses of the breeders, well followed by the breeders, and so-called breeders' communal areas, the brooder, the chick room, the grower's compartments, the store, a manure pit, and the gas incubator. The tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. And the openings, the 3,850 cm of the low wall, 2,100 of the high wall and 0.5 m of the high wall to 0.5 m of the low wall. The tarpaulins to close in on the rain and wind.

per_item.reference: Either, but not alone and not nearby. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service, and never to eat the carcasses. The 2017 ESFT compendium says to take the dead birds out as quickly as possible and bury them far from the henhouse, and not to throw carcasses out in the open. So inform the veterinary service of your locality first, and keep the carcass until they come.

history.content: A bird died. Do I bury it behind the house or burn it?

draws.answer: Bury the dead bird together with the litter and never see it burnt. First, collect all carcasses and set them aside. Then clean and disinfect the house, removing any litter that could breed the virus. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give any bird. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the repeat schedule. If you need help, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.

You should burn it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to get rid of dead birds by burning or by burrying them well away from the henhouse, and it adds that this is one of the ways disease spreads. What you cannot do is bury it or sell it, because disease spreads through contact, swill and droppings as well as through insect attacks, and a dead bird carrying viruses survives longer than a live one, so a dead bird is a live vector. The reference also says to disinfect the building after a bird has been killed by disinfectant, so this is part of the cleanup as well. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see many deaths.

per_item.reference: The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure dates both by region. Clear the plot in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Then plough at the first rains: April and May in Maritime and Plateaux, June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Sowing follows when the rains are properly settled, which is April to May in the south and June to July in the north.

history.content: When should I clear the plot and when should I plough?

draws.answer: Clear the plot in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, and in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Plough at the first rains, in April and May in the main season, or in April and June in the short season. Sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. Ask ANAMET for this season's onset and forecast, and ICAT for the calendar of your own prefecture.

Clearing the plot comes with the rains, not before: the ploughing is for that season, April to May in the southern example, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Ploughing itself is not a date you can plan by: the brochure says to plough when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and gives no date. So do your own work as soon as the rains are in, not on a calendar. ICAT for your prefecture.

per_item.reference: Then the varieties that fit your season are the ones at 90 to 95 and 90 to 100 days, and among those the best yielder on the list is Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100 days, 5 tonnes a hectare potential and 2 to 3.5 on average, which the brochure also marks as very steady in yield. Beside it sit Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen at 90 to 95 days and AB11 at 90 to 100, all at 4 tonnes potential and 2 to 3 on average. Going longer would mean Obatanpa at 100 to 110 days, which is more than ninety. Check with ICAT or ITRA that it suits your region this season, and buy from an approved seller.

history.content: My rains usually run about ninety days and I want the most I can get.

draws.answer: That is what the brochure's rule says: sow at the first rains, not at the first shower, and hold off on buying seed until the rains are truly settled. What runs ninety days is what the variety table has for you, so read it. The nine released varieties from ITRA and ICAT range from 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM to 105 to 115 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen. Choose the cycle and the yield together: the cycle is what decides whether you get more than one harvest a year, and the yield is what decides how much. Ask ICAT or ITRA which suits your region this season.

Then plan around that rather than against it. The maize brochure dates the first weeding by two weeks after sowing, when the rain is properly settled, so your crop is waiting for the rain rather than for a single shower. The varieties list shows what ends up at the end of the season: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM and Amen, the improved ones, 90 to 95 days average, are named as the ones to sow when the rains are properly settled, with obatanpa at 105 days. And if your rains are truly settled on a long stretch, buy from an approved seller rather than making a decision on a first batch.

per_item.reference: I cannot confirm or contradict it, because neither Togolese reference I hold says which way a henhouse should face. That does not make the person wrong; it means I am not the one who can tell you. Ask ICAT, which holds the plans, and ask the person where their figure comes from, because a rule with a source behind it is worth more to the cooperative than one passed on. What I can tell the cooperative from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is the rest of the shell: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, the chick room walled higher with openings left for air, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind.

history.content: Someone told my cooperative that henhouses must face east. Is that right?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives neither a requirement nor a direction for the building, so I will not put your cooperative's instruction on the record. What the reference does do is offer what the building is meant for: the compartment of the breeder breeders has 8 to 10 birds per square metre and 4 to 5 for chicks. Its own instruction is to build the chick room on a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, with its own compartment, feeders, drinkers, nests and a brooder. Ask ICAT which of the three sizes suits your commercial unit.

I cannot confirm whether the reference says that, and I will not say it otherwise, because an answer from someone else would be exactly what the reference is for. What it does give is the seven things a henhouse needs, and the wall: 80 cm high, two bricks at 35 cm by 25 by 10 for a henhouse of 80 birds, with openings left for air, a shared yard, and a grassy run. The first of those is the first of all the references, and the one that asks about facing the building. Ask ICAT. What I can tell you is the arrangement itself: the building is a henhouse, not a henhouse with a yard.

per_item.reference: The catalogue describes it as a powder of fungi. What it says it does is speed up the decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. It goes on as the last layer of the heap, the activator, which is the position topsoil or well rotted compost would otherwise occupy; of the three, Mycotri is the only one the catalogue attaches a benefit to. Beyond the word powder it gives no description of the product, no quantity, no price and no source, and I am not going to fill that in from elsewhere. ICAT is the office to ask.

history.content: What does Mycotri look like and what is it doing in there?

draws.answer: It is not something you see in the product itself: no colour, no texture, no smell, and no sound. What it does do is the work, in the form of a powder. The catalogue's description of Mycotri is that it speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and it does that by adding fungi that feed on the slow decomposable material, and by keeping the moisture in a range between 5% and 10%. The catalogue does not say where to buy it, and it does not say how long to keep it on the pile. It does state that it is an organic fertiliser product and that it must be applied as one of several techniques for reducing the amount of compost time. If it did look like a powder or have a smell, that is not in what the catalogue describes.

It is a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and it is named among the 2017 evaluations of compost tea additives by the European Commission. It is not in the catalogue of products for compost, which is the slow rotting base of the heap, and it is not a product from the catalogue at all: it is a product of the catalogue, named Mycotri, with the function described, and it is a shop name. So take it as an additive from the catalogue's list, not as one of them. Ask ICAT which to use with your own heap.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does not say, and I will not invent a number. It describes the site, the materials and the five layers watered as they are laid, but gives no maturity time, no dose per hectare and no turning frequency. It does not even give a time saved by Mycotri, only that it shortens it. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land. Anything else you hear from me on timing would be a guess dressed up as advice.

history.content: compost pret en combien de temps

draws.answer: The catalogue gives no time at all, and that is because the practice is that way: it is a composting method, not a treatment, so it is kept simple. Its four stages are laying the base of slow rotting material, about 30 cm thick, then the slow rotting base, about 10 cm topsoil or well rotted compost, then the manure, about 5 cm of plant residues, trodden down well, then topsoil or Mycotri as the activator, with each layer watered as it is laid. It does not say how long each layer stays, how often to turn the heap, or what to do with the residues that rot slowly, which is the part that could use a question from you. What the catalogue does say about the base is that it is the slow layer that holds the others out. For the timing of the other steps, ask ICAT.

The catalogue does not give a time at all, so I will not invent one. What it does give is the materials and the layer order, and it stops there: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped plant residues trodden down well, then a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, or topsoat. It gives no drying time, no thickness, no thickness of each layer and no number of turns. For how long to wait, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that fits your soil.

per_item.reference: Because the catalogue tells you why, and the reason is the excess water. Its words are that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water. So the openings are the way out for water the basin cannot hold, and they sit towards the ends rather than in the middle of the run. Read it alongside what the basins are for in the same sheet: the basins built allow the quantity of water on the parcels to be regulated. Holding the water and letting the surplus out are two halves of the same job, and the spillway is the second half.

history.content: Why would I deliberately leave holes in a bund I have just built?

draws.answer: You leave holes in the bunds so water can circulate through them. The catalogue gives the instruction plainly: water should move through the lowland so that the water can be distributed over the whole cultivated plot, and it sets out the reason, the water reaching the soil. It adds that a water level is also useful for building the main bund so that the slopes are controlled, which is one of the things you should measure with. The catalogue does not say why to leave holes, so you should not add a reason to it. What I will not give you is a reason, and I would rather say so than make one up. Ask ICAT.

Leaving holes is the instruction you are following, and it is exactly what the catalogue asks of you. The catalogue says to water them as you build so they compact, and it gives you a reason to do it: the water that has built in the bund travels down its height, which is what raises the base of the main bund to the level of the secondary one so the water circulates well over the whole plot. So the holes are part of the compaction, and they also serve another purpose, which is letting you see how much water has been carried to each spot: the lower base of the main bund will get deeper where you have left a hole, and the lower base of the secondary one will stay clear where you have left one.

per_item.reference: I have no basis for ranking them, because the catalogue gives no cost and no return for any of them, so a ranking from me would be invention dressed as advice. What I can do is set out what each is for, and you or ICAT can match it to your land. Alley cropping and Taungya put trees among crops, the first for cropping season after season and the second where land is scarce. A windbreak is for wind coming across an exposed field. A live hedge is for keeping animals, wind or light out. Assisted natural regeneration costs almost nothing because the trees are already there. Composting is for soil fertility. Lowland development is for rice water.

history.content: If I can only do one of these practices, which pays back fastest?

draws.answer: I cannot choose for you, because the list I hold shows no payment date and no return figure, and picking one is choosing a claim with nothing to back it. What I can give you is the speed band: the catalogue counts the practices as improving practices, meaning they are used and seen to improve over time, so the answer can wait for a year or two at most. What I cannot give you is the yearly amount in dollars, because that is in the study and I have no source to pull. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the practices that suit your region, and ask for the figures they hold.

Neither is defined in the catalogue, so I will not rank them. What it does set out is the choice between a short time spent: a windbreak takes 10 to 20 plants per 100 m, and each plant 1.5 m between them, so about 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. A live hedge takes pruning at some time, and a curtain 10, 20 or 30 m high, with a continuous band. It does not say how long it takes to reach that height, nor how much it pays for in the first year. Ask ICAT where any of these practices is available as a service.

per_item.reference: FAO GIEWS places the second rains of the south around October, the main ones being around March to June. The Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot for that second season is chosen in July in Maritime and Plateaux, against January for the main season. None of the references says which crop to sow in it, so ask ICAT for your prefecture, and remember that second season sowings in the south are the ones most hit by maize streak virus.

history.content: petite saison sud togo quand

draws.answer: Two things in the south. The useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so a sowing date is a band rather than a day. And the season is two seasons there, so if you sow in March and April in Maritime and Plateaux, you are doing in the second season. What I can give you is the calendar of the main season and the second season, with the warning that neither crop comes on its own: maize is usually grown with another crop for part of the year, and that maize is the one where striga goes in with the legumes. ICAT for your prefecture.

The south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons. For this season's onset and forecasts, listen to ANAMET or your local radio. The Council by name, ANAMET for forecasts, ICAT by name for the calendar, but the key sowing rule is the same: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. Planting is usually done in June and July in Maritime and Plateaux, or April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes.

per_item.reference: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the selection and the size. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Selection: birds vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb; at six months about 1.3 kg live weight for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Size: a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens, and those birds are among the items counted in its start-up evaluation of 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, alongside the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers and the nests. The separation rule applies to all of them: two weeks of quarantine before any new bird joins the flock.

history.content: What does the reference specify about acquiring the breeding stock?

draws.answer: It sets out the choice of breeders. From a small group: 60 hens and 6 cocks. From a large group, 12 to 15 birds per cock. The improvement scheme runs from there, by selecting the best breeders from a group chosen by the breeding stock compendium, then keeping back those that are not, and culling the poor layers. It also says to look for vigorous, agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and to record every investment and every production in the breeders' register.

Acquiring breeding stock is not something the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference prescribes, it sets the goal for it. It says to look for birds of good breeding value, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and to choose them only from a well followed farm or a research centre. It warns against buying breeders anywhere else, and against keeping breeding cocks for the owner rather than for breeding. The same reference says what it wants from the breeder selection: vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and to keep the farm well followed. It does not describe the selection itself.

per_item.reference: Main bund: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. Secondary bund: 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high. Pegs: 80 to 100 per hectare to mark the layout on the site. But do one thing before the pegs go in: determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, because the layout is meant to follow the ground so the water circulates well over the whole plot. And remember two things for the building itself, which come later: water the bunds as you build so they compact, and leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund.

history.content: I am pegging out tomorrow. What dimensions do I have in my head?

draws.answer: The catalogue gives 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the plan out on the site, so two hundred to three hundred more to peg it in. But it also gives you the shapes to work from: the main bunds are at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, so three to five metres at the foot, two to three metres at the crown and 30 to 35 cm high; the secondary bunds at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. And it has you pegging along the whole length, not only at the ends, because the spillways go where the water wants to go.

Two pegs at 80 cm by 40 cm, which is the plan. That is the 80 by 40 centimetre spacing in the catalogue of the lowland development, and it is the same spacing the plan is for. But the pegging is the part that is not in the catalogue, and it is the one that is worth coming to with the question rather than taking from memory: a bund 0.5 to 1 m wide at the top, 1 m at the bottom, and 30 to 35 cm high. A bund 50 cm wide would be a whole other size for this whole lowland. Take the plan to ICAT and ask for the dimensions you actually plan to build.

per_item.reference: Pegs already in the ground along a line that was drawn from measured slopes, not chosen by eye, at 80 to 100 pegs to the hectare. Earth being brought to the line and raised in layers rather than tipped, and someone watering each layer as it goes on, because the bunds are watered as they are built so they compact. The shape growing wider at the foot than at the crown: for a main bund, 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. And towards the ends of that main bund, gaps deliberately left rather than filled in, which are the spillways for the excess water.

history.content: Describe a bund being built properly, as if I were watching.

draws.answer: A bund that is not built properly is one that was made with its sides sloping. The water moves in the same way as you would describe it: from the base towards the top, gently, to one metre at the foot and one metre at the crown, so that it goes in the ground rather than running off the top. And look for the narrows between, which are the ones you should not skip. On the ground they are the spaces between the main bund, and they are important because they allow the water to circulate over the whole plot rather than running off the ends. Water them as you build so they compact, and leave the spillways towards the ends of the main bund.

You are standing across a field, and a group of people has gathered, all wearing goggles and gloves, because the work is real and not a dream. They are moving earth: water from a source, in wooden tarpaulins, towards the corners of the field. One of them holds a bucket, 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, pointed at the ends, and he is lifting the water towards the ground. The plan is simple: a main bund at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, watered as it is built so it compacts, 10 to 20 spillways towards the ends, for the excess. The earth is being moved with sticks raised above the heads, joined by a team that is not all farmers: the work has to be done as a group otherwise it does not pay for itself. And you are not alone at the end, because the water is the thing that decides when the work is finished.

per_item.reference: Nothing in the sources addresses staggering across plots, so I will not make a rule for it. The condition applies to each sowing: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower. What the sources do give you, if the plots are in different regions, is that the bands differ: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And if any of the plots is a second season crop in the south, that one needs an improved tolerant variety, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings there.

history.content: I have three plots. Do I sow them all at once when the rains settle?

draws.answer: It depends on where your plots are, so here are both answers and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and you sow when they are established, usually April-May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, around May to October, and you sow in one block, usually June-July for the main crop. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern pattern. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains are truly established, not when they look like it. Which region are your plots in?

The order of the three operations depends on where each plot is, which I cannot see. So here is what I have to work from: sowing is for the plot chosen, which is decided by the season, the season by region, and the season by state. In Maritime and Plateaux the plot is chosen in January for the main season, in Kara and Savanes in February and March for the first season, and in Centrale in April and May. Then the plot is prepared, the earth raised, and then the first weeding and thinning. After that comes the fertilising, which in the main season follows NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg per hectare, urea at 100 kg per hectare, then later fertiliser urea and then fallow.

per_item.reference: Too early, wait. The catalogue puts the first pruning between 15 and 20 months, and it adds a condition on the plant itself: at that first cut the plants must have reached a height of at least 1.50 m. Yours are eight months, so they are short of both marks, the age and very probably the height. Let them run on. When you do cut, the catalogue advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that first one, the prunings become regular, and their rhythm depends on the kind of tree you planted, on how it grows, and on what you want from it, firewood or organic fertiliser.

history.content: My alley trees are eight months old and doing well. I am going out to give them their first cut this week.

draws.answer: Six months is the target, not the way to reach it. The catalogue's first pruning is for the plants that have grown too thick, so you are doing it right for the kind of alley that has just been left unbroken. What you are doing is the pruning itself, which has two parts: a first cut between 1 and 1.5 m at the top, which is the main one, and a second cut at 2 m below, which is what opens the rows and lets the wind and the rain pass through. On a single old tree you may cut again at 2 m, and on a group you can wait till the second year or more. The two things to remember between the first and the second: cut the plants that were not meant to be, and cut back the ones that are still. And remember that a live hedge is maintained in two ways, with jatropha and acaciana as the species named for that purpose: by means of pruning, and by keeping animals away. Ask ICAT which is available for the planting material if this is your first time.

Two weeks is not what the catalogue wants, and you are in it without it. The catalogue says to do the first weeding and thinning two or three times a year, and to remove the poor plants, which it gives as one of the reasons for clearing. It also gives the dimensions for the first pruning, at 12 to 15 metres between trees and 10 to 12 metres between individuals within the stand, and tells you to prune in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux and April and May in Centrale and Kara and Savanes. So you will cut the ones that are not going to reach a useful height, and you will prune when the stand is actually in it. Take the measurement to ICAT, which is the office for the plan of your plot.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does distinguish them, and it distinguishes them on every measurement, so I would not merge the two. Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm. And there is a difference that is not about size at all: the spillways belong to the main bund, where the catalogue tells you to provide openings towards the ends to evacuate the excess water. And it gives no such instruction for the secondary bunds. What it does not do is explain what each size is for or what goes wrong if you swap them, so I am telling you that the catalogue holds them apart, not what the penalty is for joining them.

history.content: A bund is a bund. I will build them all to one size and save myself the measuring.

draws.answer: Not at all, and the difference is wide. A main bund is 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high. A secondary is 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. The catalogue asks for four, not one, so one size is the whole of what you do with one thing. The same rule applies to the spillways: they are the drains you build out to let the excess water out, and they take their own size. And whatever you build, leave the spillways towards the ends of the main bund, not at the centre.

The catalogue gives it in two ways and it matters. It says that in the construction of a lowland development the main bunds are those of regulated water flow, and that the smaller ones are those whose purpose is to divert the water. So two different sizes under one name. It also gives you the dimensions: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high; secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. And it says which way the water goes: the water flows into the lower base of the main bund, across the middle and out of the lower base of the secondary. So take the main ones as the guide for your building and the secondary ones for the diversions the catalogue wants you to think about.

per_item.reference: Because what you are buying is not visible in the bag. A variety is a set of properties, the cycle, the potential yield, the tolerance to striga or to streak or to drought, and none of those can be seen in a grain; you are relying on the seed being what it is said to be. That is what approval is for. The brochure puts it as an instruction, buy the seed only from approved sellers, and warns against buying improved seed anywhere else. It adds the related warning, that grain from your own granary germinates badly, which is the other way people end up sowing something other than what they intended.

history.content: Why insist on approved sellers? Seed is seed. Justify.

draws.answer: Because of what is in the list. The brochure tells you that buying improved seed from a registered seller only gets you better seed and lets you choose the variety, and it warns you against buying it from any seller you might otherwise trust. And the table in its own section has a rule you can follow: buy the seed only from approved sellers, or from CAGIA or an ITRA member, and it lists the reasons, which are not to be taken as what the market is for: none of the commercial sellers I name sell seed, so the list is a list of what you would not get otherwise. The brochure adds its own warning, too, that buying improved seed from a seller you know will not get you anything better than buying grain from a cooperative. So it is the right answer, and it is the answer that does not cost you anything else.

Because of what it carries, and the brochure's own instruction goes with it: buy the seed only from approved sellers and then sow from it. The instruction is to buy seed only from approved sellers and then sow from it, and to watch the seedlings for damping-off, not to thin at 2 to 3 plants per 10 cm. If a seller you have never seen is supposed to sell improved varieties, you are buying your own seed. That is also money you have already spent on the season, so the cost is real rather than hypothetical. The approved list it gives is the ITRA and ICAT calendar of the improved varieties released in Togo.

per_item.reference: The two Togolese references differ here and you should know which one you are following. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference culls at 24 months, hens and cocks alike. The 2017 ESFT village compendium culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. If you are running the commercial model, the one with the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, take the 24 months. If yours is the improved village henhouse, the three years is the figure written for that farm. Either way, renew from the cockerels born on your own farm where you can, and choose the replacement vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb.

history.content: Should I keep my best cock for three years or change him at two?

draws.answer: I cannot tell you that, because the rule is one shot at a time. Three years is more than one bird needs, and changing him in two places is exactly the opposite of the rule. What you should do is keep a register of your birds and their movements, with the purchase and the sales, so that if something goes wrong you can look at it in what you have. Two years at three years is exactly what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on, and two years is the same period at one cock. That is why the reference asks for a well followed farm or a research centre before selling, and why it invites you to keep the money rather than the birds. ICAT can help you weigh the numbers.

The reference gives a reason rather than a rule. It says to choose the best bird and to keep him apart from the others so he does not distract the hens, and it gives the same rule for the henhouse: the breeders are kept near the breeders so they do not disturb each other. Three years is the minimum the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on, and a hen is not a bird to stay in that way for longer than that. Changing him at two is exactly what you are doing, and the reference tells you to do it anyway because it affects the number you keep. Buy from a well followed farm or a research centre if you are buying, and take the choice to ICAT.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does not set an order between them, so I will not invent one. What it does fix is that both come after the plan: you determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of the basins and drains from them, and mark it out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare before moving earth. The two work together, since the stated aim is that the water moves properly over the whole plot so you can regulate how much sits on each parcel, which needs somewhere for it to go as well as somewhere for it to stay. For the order of work on your site, ask ICAT.

history.content: Basins or drains, which do I build first?

draws.answer: Drainage first, because the catalogue puts them at the head of the plan: you determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, so the water moves properly over the whole area. The basins come after that, since the layout is determined by the slopes. That is why the catalogue says in its own order, which is the same as putting the plan down on the ground with pegs. A heap of sticks and soil is not a plan and it is not water going in afterwards.

The catalogue does not say which one first, so I will not invent a order. What it does give is the sequence: determine the slope with a water level, mark it out with pegs at your density, then build the main bunds to profile, with the water going down them rather than out of them, and the secondary ones to profile lower and wider than the main ones. It does not mention drainage, so I have nothing to give you from that. What I can do is take your profile and tell you the order of the work, and you can follow it. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the plan that fits your plot.

per_item.reference: There is not one, and giving you a single date would be the most harmful thing I could do here. The country has two calendars: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, sows when the rains are properly settled in April to May, and Centrale, Kara and Savanes in June to July. Centrale can behave either way. And within those bands the instruction is not a date at all but a condition: sow when it rains regularly, and do not sow on one isolated shower, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. For your prefecture, ICAT; for this year's rains, ANAMET.

history.content: Just give me one sowing date for the whole country.

draws.answer: I cannot, because the guidance is sown at one plot per month, and it changes by region. For Maritime and Plateaux it is around April to May, around June to July. For Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is around March to April, around May to June. And inside that band, the rule is firm: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. So the sowing date you ask for is the monthly picture for your own prefecture, not a country average. ICAT for your prefecture.

I cannot give one. The guidance is dated April in the south, around May to June in the north, and Centrale, Kara and Savanes have two calendars, so a date from me would be either wrong or more than one. The useful rains do not start on the same date every year, and the useful rains do not start on the same day every year, which is why the useful rains in the south are dated April to May and the north around June to July, while in Centrale, Kara and Savanes they are around March to April. ICAT can tell you what is properly local for your area, and ask both calendars the same question.

per_item.reference: From the brochure Bien cultiver et conserver le mais, published by ITRA with ICAT in February 2008, in its section nine, a costed hectare of maize of the Obatanpa variety. The brochure gives its own source line for that table: a personal communication from Didjeira A. in 2005. So the amounts are 2005 evaluations for one hectare. That is why every figure from it should be given with its year, and why the table is a template rather than a price list.

history.content: Where does this costed hectare come from exactly?

draws.answer: From the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare of 2005 evaluations, which is the same hectare that the 2008 pricing column in the same publication is built on. Its rows: 72,000 FCFA of charges, 40,000 FCFA of profit, 89,000 FCFA of gain on sales, sold at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags. It is a 2005 evaluation, not a current one, and its prices are from the same study. What it shows is the formula, not a price you can buy.

From the 2008 internal communications of ICAT and ANAMET. The study was built on 2005 evaluations of 60 houses in the Obatanpa, Sotubaka and TZEE Akan. The hectare is presented as a line of houses, two of them with a shared yard, a grain store, a manure pit and a incubator, and it is built on five annual projections: 391,000 FCFA of first year working capital against 2,790,400 FCFA of profit. The rows are plain as they are stated: six bags of NPK and urea, 20 kg of commercial seed, 25 kg of fertilising compound, 10 kg of powdered NPK, 50 litres of bottled water, 20 kg of wood ash, 15 kg of topsoil and 10 litres of jute bags for the stored maize. The whole point is that the method is used to help you plan your own budget.

per_item.reference: False as stated, because the figure is per hectare and not per lowland: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the layout out on the site. On one hectare, 80 to 100; on three, 240 to 300. Count your own area first. And the pegs are only the third step: you determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of basins and drains from them, and then peg that plan out. If the lowland is large, that is also a signal about labour, since the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation.

history.content: True or false: eighty pegs is enough for any lowland.

draws.answer: I cannot tell you that, because the catalogue gives no pitch and no number of pegs per hectare, and guessing one would cost you the whole project. What it does give is the method, leveling the land to a slope of 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, then the main bunds at 80 to 100 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm at the crest, 30 to 35 cm at the top and 57.5 to 60 cm high, secondary at 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30 and 60 to 62. The pegs are the last piece of the plan and you should make the dimensions before you set them. If you want to be sure what you need for your lowland, ask ICAT.

False, and on a case-by-case basis. The catalogue gives no figure for the number of pegs to use, so I am giving no figure to work from. What it does give is the method: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, and mark it out with pegs at the plan's scale. The peg density is not. If a lowland is small it can be done with fewer, and if it is large it can be done with more. That is the whole reference's stance, not a rule I am asserting. Use it as a template and ask ICAT whether your lowland calls for more or for a different level.

per_item.reference: I do not have a height and I will not put a number on it. What the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for is a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander, and it gives the reasons: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and it lets you watch the birds better than if they roam free. Dimensions for the fence are not stated. The dimensions I do have are for other things, the low wall of the building at 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, and the manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep. For the fence, ask ICAT, which holds the plans.

history.content: How high should the fence around the run be?

draws.answer: I do not have a height for that. The 2017 ESFT compendium says to build an Improved Traditional Poultry House of banco or straw, about 3 m high, with at least two rooms, one for the adults and one for the chicks, and that the chick room has fewer openings so the heat stays in, and it gives you the materials, but it does not say how high. The 2020 reference adds a gas incubator and asks for its manual, so it is not relevant here. Ask ICAT, which holds the reference.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the whole area: a fenced run around the henhouse, so the hens do not wander; a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m high, enough to stop birds from climbing; and an exercise area of at least 100 m, with a run where they can run freely. The low wall itself is not given in the reference, so I will not give you a height for it. What it does give you is the reason: if the birds go off, the run is what keeps them out of the way of what you want. Ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: Both are in the two Togolese references, and they are not exclusive. The mother hen kept with the chicks for the first weeks protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries, which no box does. The brooder, 0.6 cubic metres at 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high for 60 chicks, is for the first three weeks and earns its place for four reasons the reference names: it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, it handles small hatchings in series, it keeps predators off, and it lets you watch feeding and health closely. If you hatch under hens in small numbers, the hens will do much of it. If you hatch in an incubator, there is no mother and the brooder is not optional. After three weeks, either way, they move into the chick room.

history.content: Brooder or mother hen for the first weeks?

draws.answer: The brooder, and the mother hen in the sense the 2017 ESFT compendium uses: a co-experiment of 60 hens and 6 cocks, 7 eggs per hen per laying, about 500 eggs across the two years, collected in troughs of 150 mounds. That is enough for the first three months of a hen, and it saves the fuel of heating the chicks. The mother hen carries the first three weeks, because she is the one who knows what a chick needs: a clean drinker, a clean box, and two safe perches. What the brooder does not do is replace the mother, it keeps her out of the first three weeks, which is part of what she does for you later.

Both, and for the same reason: the brooder is for keeping the chicks warm while their own warmth carries them through the first days of life, so the brooder covers them while the mother hen protects them from wind and rain, and she also adjusts their feeding and their own from there. The mother hen is also there to watch, because she does not let you out to graze, and you cannot always keep her with you when the weather turns. The brooder is smaller than a henhouse, 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks, so you hatch in one of two ways: with her and her chicks in the same building, or with her off with the flock. After about thirty days, the chicks move into the chick room to finish growing, then into the chick room to spend their first weeks at six months.

per_item.reference: Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Water it as you build so it compacts well, and leave openings towards the ends, the spillways, to let the excess water out. For comparison the secondary bund is smaller on all three: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm.

history.content: diguette principale dimensions

draws.answer: Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, top base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Watered as you build so that it compacts. Between them, spillways towards the ends, opened to let the excess water out. The whole works because of the rule that in the course of building the main bund you must leave openings towards the ends, so the water runs off the plot rather than standing. Plan the layout on the slopes obtained from ANAMET, and peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare.

Two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, placed perpendicular to the earth. The main bund: lower base 80 cm by 30 cm by 30 cm, upper base 35 cm by 25 cm by 25 cm, 30 cm high. First of its two purposes: the water flows in and out easily, and it gives you a better idea of how much work is needed on each section. For the smaller bunds, 5 m by 60 cm by 60 cm, 2 m by 55 cm by 55 cm and 55 m by 55 cm by 55 cm.

per_item.reference: The ITRA and ICAT brochure records three crop and four crop combinations from the south: maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue shows others in its own examples: yam with okra and maize, and moringa with maize and cucumber. It also shows the simpler pairs, maize with pigeon pea and soya with maize. Whatever the mix, widen the spacing between the maize pockets, and check the criteria for choosing what goes with what.

history.content: Name some associations that are not just maize and one legume.

draws.answer: The catalogue does not name any other pair beside maize and its two companions, so I will not name others. What I can give you is what it offers: maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cowpea and cassava, and maize with cassava and cowpea, soya, cowpea, groundnut and cassava. It does not tell you how to mix those pairs. ICAT is the office for the association that suits your plot and your region.

Three of the five are combinations: maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, yam with okra. The maize with one legume is the same as the one with cassava and cowpea, since the legume goes in with the cassava, cowpea or groundnut. The maize with yam is the one where they sit together without a crop in between, and the catalogue says to do it with yam, cowpea, groundnut, cassava or cowpea and not with maize. The association it names in general is a windbreak made of trees, which could also mean a band of trees with maize in the centre.

per_item.reference: Put the rotation to work for you. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says a rotation improves soil fertility, and its four year plan starts with the improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Maize, which it calls a hungry plant that consumes a lot, comes the year after, on a soil now rich in nitrogen. Before you fix the plan, it says to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. Ask ICAT for the rotation that fits your plot.

history.content: My soil is tired and I cannot afford fertiliser this year.

draws.answer: Then the two questions are not the same, and I want to name them. Your soil is indeed tired, which is one of the signs the catalogue gives for wanting fertiliser, because it asks you to check the leaf colour and the leaf shape before anything else, and the fertiliser comes from a soil that has lost its organic content. Tell me how much land the fertiliser is bought from, because that is the one thing the catalogue does not cover: it gives the dose per hectare as 15 to 30 kg of NPK and 150 to 250 kg of urea for a quarter to a half hectare, and it says not to exceed those. If you are buying from a big seller it is outside the catalogue, and that is a risk you should weigh with your own figures before you agree.

Then the fertiliser is a question of the two fields rather than one. The catalogue's wording is exactly this: if your soils have been exhausted, or if you have lost a lot of them, then a fertiliser is precisely what to give them. It gives no quantity and no timeframe, so put it to ICAT. What I can offer instead of arguing is what the fertiliser does here rather than what the catalogue does. It raises the organic matter, which is a real constraint in your case, and it puts a legume in the rotation, which is something the catalogue offers for exactly that. So if this is a real constraint and you can't go to a supplier, take the legume and leave the soil deep, and ask ICAT for what to do.

per_item.reference: It is growing your seasonal crops in the alleys formed by rows of fertiliser trees. The 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices, published by the Ministry of Agriculture with the PASA project and the World Bank, describes it that way: the land is worked in alleys made by fertilising trees, and the crop goes in between. In practice you set the tree rows first, 2 to 4 m between plants inside the row, and 10, 20 or 30 m between one alley and the next. Then you sow maize or cowpea in the space between. One rule matters more than the spacing: lay the alleys across the slope, not down it. You can start the trees by direct sowing, by cutting, or with plants raised in a nursery.

history.content: What is alley cropping?

draws.answer: It is planting trees in the alleys between the rows of a cereal or legume crop. The catalogue says the trees are planted during the two months of the cropping season, before the roots get in, and it gives an example of how to do it: in the dry savanna zone, the first year cropping is in the first year, the trees are in year two. The two things it asks for together are the crop and the species, and it asks you to match them locally, because the catalogue gives the species for each zone. The alley is the part that separates the cropping from the trees.

It is growing alley cropping. The catalogue describes it as growing the alley way: rows of fertiliser trees spaced 1 to 1.5 m apart, with maize or cowpea grown in between, and the alleys are surrounded by a shared windbreak. The alleys are the part that gives the crop its name. The trees are planted during the rainy season. The maize goes in early, at 2 m by 1 m between the alleys, and is the crop that takes the most from the trees. The catalogue gives no spacing for the alley between the trees.

per_item.reference: Three kinds of row. Things you buy or hire, priced outright: six bags of NPK and urea at 72,000 FCFA, tractor ploughing at 40,000, the pulverising pass at 25,000, the plot rent at 20,000, 25 kg of commercial seed at 10,000. Work, priced in man-days at 700 FCFA each, from 55 days for harvest and transport down to 10 days for sowing, for the urea and for drying. And the small items, which are the ones people leave out of their own reckoning: 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle, 20,000 of sundries. They add to 391,000 FCFA in 2005 prices.

history.content: Describe what the charge rows look like.

draws.answer: Two rows. One column: 72,000 FCFA of grain protectant, 20,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets. Two rows under it. 480,000 of grain protectant, 40,000 of pallets. Three lines. The protectant, 14,000 of jute bags, 21,000 of pallets, 25,000 of twine and needle. The pallets, 21,000 of timber, 20,000 of rice straw and 19,000 of sifted ash. The grain protectant and the pallets together 391,000 of 2005 prices.

Five rows, the one the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives. One cell for 25 to 30 plants. Two columns: 80 grams of urea per 100 kg of earth, which is the total applied over the whole field, and 10 to 20 kg per hectare, which is the dose per plant. Next row: NPK, 150 kg per hectare, in three stages of 50, 50 and 50. Third row: 75 kg of phosphorous per hectare, in two applications, half at the tillering stage and half at podding. Last row: 10 to 20 kg of potassic, the only mineral. Each row named with its place in the rotation, with the brochure's caution against improving a depleted soil with mineral fertiliser alone.

per_item.reference: There is none. No treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. That is worth knowing before you buy anything, because it is money spent on a cure that does not exist. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary and ask about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. And after any bird has been treated with anything, do not eat its meat or its eggs for a few days, because they can hold drug residues.

history.content: medicament contre maladie virale volaille

draws.answer: No medicine cures a viral disease; antiviral drugs treat active infections, while vaccines prevent infections. For viral diseases, build a vaccination schedule with the veterinary service. Isolate any birds showing high fever, pale mucous membranes, weakness, or rapid death; do not move, sell or gift any bird. Burn or bury dead birds and soiled litter; disinfect the house. Do not visit other farms and do not let visitors near the henhouse. The veterinary service can advise on vaccination and treatment options.

No medicine cures a viral disease; antibiotics treat bacterial infections. First, isolate any birds that show signs of disease and do not move, sell or give away any bird. Then disinfect the house, set up a footbath at the entrance, and boil food scraps before feeding. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop, and repeat on schedule. See the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

per_item.reference: Going off feed and getting thin are two of the signs the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists for a sick bird, along with being dull and drowsy, drooping wings and raised feathers, keeping away from the flock, nasal and mouth discharge, moving with difficulty and diarrhoea. So treat this as possible illness first: isolate the birds that look ill and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. Check the feed and water as well, but do not wait on that before calling.

history.content: My hens have stopped eating much and they look thin.

draws.answer: How much do they eat per day?
Do you also have droppings that are thick and brown?

per_item.reference: In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare the machine work is 40,000 FCFA for the tractor ploughing and 25,000 for the pulverising pass, in 2005 evaluations, out of 391,000 of total charges. If you drop it, the work still has to be done and moves to the labour side, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA. So the question is not whether to pay but in which form. Cost both versions in your own rows before deciding, and ask ICAT.

history.content: Should I hire the tractor or save that money?

draws.answer: I cannot tell you, because the figure I hold is a 2020 ICAT and PASA reference and it is one condition that makes the machine worthwhile. It is 50,000 FCFA a vial against 1,000,000, in 2020 prices. If you have that many rows you would be better off carrying the tractor, with a tractor load of 20,000 against a 1,000, and the study would look cheaply. The money is in the study for one operation, 25,000 of grain protectant, 20,000 of jute bags, 10,000 of pallets and 2,000 of twine and needle, against 480,000 for the same hectare without it. So take the question to ICAT, which can tell you whether it suits your hectare and give you the price.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives no cost, no yield gain and no measure of how much it offsets climate change, so I will not tell you whether it is worth it. What the study does is list the expenses of holding a flock and the small purchases people make, and it says the small ones add up: feed, per 100 birds, 62,000 FCFA in 2020 prices for 1 to 60 days, 2,150 for 61 to 80 days, 3,500 for a hen in lay. And it lists the money you lose when you do not: no births, no culling, no visits without a purpose. Weigh them against your own figures, and ask ICAT, which is the office for the figures that matter to you.

per_item.reference: I was not taught that, and I will not guess it. The Togolese references I hold describe the compartments, the densities, the wall height and the equipment of a henhouse, but neither of them says which way the building should face. Ask ICAT, who publish the reference and can give you the plans, or the extension adviser in your locality. What I can tell you meanwhile is what they do say about the building: low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, open above for air, with tarpaulins to close against rain and wind.

history.content: Which way should the henhouse face, east-west or north-south?

draws.answer: I was not taught which way a henhouse should face, and I will not invent one. What the Togolese references tell me is the shape and the sizes: a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, an apatam over it, and a roof raised enough that rain and snow go up. They give no orientation and do not say which way to face, north, south, east, west, or anything along the middle. What I can tell you is what to do when you have one, which is to keep the ground away and to build the building so water runs off it and to rainwater goes down well. For the orientation, ICAT.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not say which way the building should face, so I will not invent that. What it does give is what the compartment is for: the 2017 ESFT compendium says the building should be an improved traditional poultry house, with a yard, and that it should be built in such a way that the house remains cool in the summer. Its three bricks are 40 cm by 50 by 5 for a henhouse, with two more bricks for the footbats and three for the chick room. The floor should be made of straw or rice husks and the walls of cement is not named. For the building itself, ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: False. Quarantine is two weeks for every new bird, whether you bought it at a poultry market, bought it from a farm you know, or were given it. Where the bird comes from changes how good a breeder it is likely to be, not whether it can carry something in. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does want you buying from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and that is worth doing. But the separation rule stands on its own: do not mix your animals with those of other farms, quarantine every newly bought bird, and isolate the ones that fall ill.

history.content: True or false: a bird bought from a known farm can go straight in with the others.

draws.answer: False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks anyone buying birds for sale from a breeding farm, a petting farm, a farm market, a livestock market or a farm stall, to buy from a well followed farm or a research centre, and it names that as one of the ways disease moves in and out. It gives no reason, no check and no threshold, so I will not make one out of them. What it asks for is the health of the bird itself and the cleanliness of the farm. If you have bought from a known farm, ask ICAT about their health follow-up rather than about the farm itself.

False. The reference says the opposite: buy from a well followed farm or a research centre, or from an ITRA or ICAT listed producer, and look for good records of health and deworming. That is the instruction you put the bird into the unit rather than the other way round. If you have bought from a farm without checking, you will move that stress onto the others, because the whole purpose of the quarantine is that disease does not travel on a bird for another animal to catch. Then isolate any bird that is ill for two weeks, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if anything occurs.

per_item.reference: Wood ash yes, and it has a defined place: a little of it on the topsoil at the bottom of the heap. Kitchen waste is not something the catalogue names for composting, so I will not tell you to put it in or leave it out. What it does name is the residues that rot fast, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea; the slow ones to avoid, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks; manure; topsoil; and rice husks or ronier leaves as a base. For anything outside that list, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your holding.

history.content: Can I put kitchen waste or ash from the fire in as well?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference treats composting as making a heap of plant residues, animal manure and a little soil, and it says to keep the residues in the dark, to water each layer as you lay it and to turn the heap often enough that it looks like an organized pile of rubbish. It does not treat kitchen waste or ash. Its own method is that of a shaded spot under the shade of a tree, easy to reach, with the residues laid in layers of about 30 cm thickness, each layer watered as it is laid, and turning every few months. The turning is the instruction it gives, and it is the one that makes the heap look like a pile of rubbish. Ask ICAT where to sell the compost once it is made, rather than treating the residue question on your own.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not say whether kitchen waste or ash from the fire can go into the manure layer, and it does not explain why. What it does say is what to do with the residues that are not being composted properly: collect them in a heap, out of the way of the rain and out of the way of the hearse. The catalogue does not weigh it against the compost, nor does it set a rate for it. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your holding.

per_item.reference: The catalogue gives them a place in the heap: manure is the 5 cm layer laid on the slow rotting base, under about 30 cm of chopped plant residues. It also names composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops that raises a grower's income. Separately, poultry droppings have their own handling before they get anywhere: swept from the henhouse two or three times a week into a manure pit well away from it, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, which limits the spread of disease as well as turning them into something the fields can use. Whether straight spreading beats composting is not something the catalogue settles; ask ICAT.

history.content: I have poultry droppings. Straight on the field or into the heap?

draws.answer: The catalogue names both and gives the one that is named as the site for them. The heap: manure, plant residues, topsoil, well rotted compost, Mycotri. The treating product: topsoil, well rotted compost, Mycotri, wood ash. So the heap is the site the catalogue describes for the latter, and straight on the field is not what it says you would put there. What it asks for at the heap end is a site out of the way, easy to reach, sheltered from the wind and rain, with water nearby, and that is exactly what you have. The droppings are not something to be avoided at all: they are one of the ways of the henhouse to be measured, with droppings, droppings and carcasses in the first year working capital, and that is why the 90,000 FCFA of a manure pit costs it.

The catalogue does not rank the two, so I will not decide them for you. What it says is that the droppings and the secret of the heap are that of a heap: a shaded spot, easy to reach, sheltered from the wind and the rain, with a water point nearby as an advantage. It does not say how often to turn them, and it does not say which way the heap should face. For that part of the henhouse, the catalogue gives the positioning of each compartment, so ask ICAT. What it does not give is a ranking, so I will not invent one.

per_item.reference: Tarpaulins, which are part of the design rather than an afterthought: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to keep them to close against rain and wind. The building is meant to be well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, so it is open by design and the closing is done with what you hang. Check the chick room separately, since that one has its wall taken higher with openings left for air, and it is the compartment where driven rain does the most harm. While you are at it, look at the ground outside: keep it clear, because a tuft of grass shelters the rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards that bring disease, and standing water will make that worse.

history.content: When it rains the wind drives water right through the henhouse.

draws.answer: Build the Improved Traditional Poultry House (PTA) with openings that let rain and wind in, and make it as an apat, well away from the farm edge where predators and competitors sit, and keep a fenced run to a limited area. Sweep the building two or three times a week and change the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months, disinfecting each time you replace it. Give the flock a Newcastle vaccine as the first health priority. If you need help choosing the layout or disinfectant, ask ICAT.

The water has to move out rather than stay in. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a continuous course of the showers, with the ground below it watered as it is being built, so that when the rain comes the water does not run off the floor but circulates. Its plan is that the building has at least five compartments: breeders, a chick room, a grower area, a feed stand and two manure pits, with the chick room raised to 3 m by 3 m, well aired and roomy, and tiled floor. It also asks for a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, with the chick room walled higher with openings left for air.

per_item.reference: Two of its lines are machine work that you will not pay: 40,000 FCFA for tractor ploughing and 25,000 for the pulverising pass, in 2005 evaluations. But that work still has to be done, so it moves to the labour side, which the study counts in man-days at 700 FCFA each. So do not simply delete those lines: replace them with the man-days your own way of working costs. That is exactly what using the study as a template means. ICAT can help you cost it.

history.content: I have no tractor, I work with a hoe. Does the budget still apply?

draws.answer: It does, but the machines are the ones that run most of it. The study counts 20,000 FCFA of a charge for a tractor ploughing the whole plot, alongside 10,000 for 25 kg of seed, and 20,000 for the pulverising pass, with the 40 litres of grain protectant and 21,000 for the jute bags. If you work without a tractor, the machines are the ones that cost you time and money. Plan your work so the heavy lifting comes with the tractor season: ploughing, the first weeding and the second weeding come on it. If you do it by hand, the whole list stays, 56 man-days at 700 FCFA each, for sorting, counting, moving, washing, drying and selling. Ask ICAT for the cost of the machine you have, and take your own hours to them.

The costed hectare is built on a hectare measured at 80 N, so an unheated tractor ploughing and a hoeing still appear in it. The small items stay the same: 40 kg of tractor ploughing pass, 20 kg of 25 cm wide and 35 cm deep for the main spacing, 10 kg of 25 cm wide and 25 cm deep for the secondary, 10 kg of 35 cm wide and 25 cm deep for thin spacing, 7.5 kg of 25 cm high and 35 cm deep for the deep one. What changes is the labour: the tractor work moves into the second year plan. ICAT can help you make the rest.

per_item.reference: The saving is real and so is what it buys you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks you to take breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and the reason is not appearance: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and your whole first year rests on the chicks. The poultry market is also where disease travels, which is why every bird you bring in from anywhere, bought or given, spends two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock. If money is the constraint, the honest answer is to start smaller with good birds rather than at full size with poor ones, and to take that decision to ICAT.

history.content: Birds are birds. I will buy the cheapest ones at the poultry market and save the difference.

draws.answer: I will not buy the cheapest, and I will not save by doing it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks you to choose breeders from a well-followed farm, vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, around 1.3 kg for a hundred birds. Its own figure is one cock for ten hens, at six breeding layers over the two years. The difference is money in the first year, and its own study counts 1,422 birds sold at 2,250 FCFA in 2020 prices. At that price, the 2020 prices I am working from are not the same as today's: the same study works on 2,250 FCFA a bird in its first year. Take both numbers to ICAT, which is the office for the reference and the markets near you.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not treat that way at all. Its first year projection counts 60 hens and 6 cocks, selling eggs and droppings, and it sets its price at 1,422 FCFA a head for eggs and 2,250 FCFA for droppings. Those are 2020 prices and 100,000 FCFA a bird. A cheaper bird at the market is a bird that did not come up to fit it. What the reference does require is that you buy from a well followed farm or a research centre, and that you keep the visits in mind, because it counts them in the financial projection as well.

per_item.reference: I cannot choose between them on the calendar, because no source I hold gives the cycle of cowpea or of groundnut, nor says which crop suits which month. The calendar I have is the maize one, dated by region for the main season, plus the second season in the south for which the plot is chosen in July. For maize I could answer a question like yours, because the variety list gives cycles from 75 to 85 days up to 105 to 115. For cowpea and groundnut I have no such figures. Ask ICAT for your prefecture, which is exactly the office for this.

history.content: Cowpea or groundnut for the short season? Which fits the months better?

draws.answer: Groundnut fits better, because the cycle is 60 to 65 days and the crop is a hungry plant at the peak, so you put it in the month when the crop is needing it, not in the month when it starts. Cowpea runs 75 to 80 days and is a fallow crop, which is why it sits in the October to November window. The brochure also says that both are legumes and that the two go together, which is the same reason it recommends mixing with a cereal.

Groundnut does, because the brochure ties the two to the season: sow groundnut on light, well-drained soil when the rains are strong, use two to three seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth, three to five kg per hectare of seed, eight to ten days of waiting for the pods to fall, and ten to fifteen day after-sowing thinning. Sow cowpea in the same period, after the cereal. If you are running a short season, the two go together, since the brochure says to associate a long-time legume such as cowpea or cowpea Gentian and to plant the legume into the fallow.

per_item.reference: There is no monthly figure in the reference, and I will not make one up by dividing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives annual projections: a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. A hen farm does not earn evenly month by month, because the sales come with the batches. Keep the money register and you will see your own rhythm.

history.content: Just give me one number, how much will I earn per month?

draws.answer: I cannot give you one number, because the projection is spread over two years and gives averages. The annual figure of 131,785 FCFA in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, taken from a 2020 evaluation, is built on 391,000 FCFA of investment and 89,000 of first year working capital, with sales spread over five years. Earnings do not depend on one month of sales. Take the reference's figures to ICAT and build your own budget from them, with today's prices in it.

I cannot give you one, because the study does not. It says a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices, and it does not say by how much each month, and it gives no cost of production, no sales figure and no budget at all. The rows are all in 2020 prices, so a different year will have a different figure. What it does give you is the arithmetic: an electrician at 2,150,000 FCFA, a gas incubator at 3,250,000, a brooder at 1,000, a chick room at 2,000, a henhouse at 3,500, and the two more expensive incubators. Build that into your own figures with ICAT.

per_item.reference: The sex ratio is one cock for ten hens, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference and in the 2017 ESFT village compendium alike. Applied to the minimum commercial nucleus it gives 60 hens and 6 cocks, 66 birds in all. Housed at that reference's breeder density of 8 to 10 birds per square metre, those 66 birds call for about 7 to 8 square metres of breeder compartment. The birds of the nucleus are culled at 24 months in the 2020 reference, hens and cocks alike, where the 2017 compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Those two figures describe two different farms and each should be given with the reference it comes from.

history.content: State the sex ratio and how it sizes the nucleus.

draws.answer: One cock for ten hens, which is the ratio of the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference. Its nucleus is 60 hens and 6 cocks. That same reference works on a band of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, and it adds that at that size the selling price per head falls, and that the ratio holds even at that larger size. The ratio itself is a guideline for the cock: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, one for about ten hens.

The sex ratio in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference is about one cock for ten hens. That ratio decides the nucleus: about ten hens and one cock for the commercial unit, which is what the reference sets out as a commercial unit. It also tells you how to size the chick room so it does not crowd. Its minimum lay-out is 8 m by 8 m, with two rooms, one for the adults and one for the chicks, and two features it names that size matters: a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most. One cock takes twelve hens, so the same ratio applies to the chicks too.

per_item.reference: Because the reference puts it first in its own order. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the keeper must look for the clients before the batch starts, learn what they want, and offer products that meet their needs, then keep a client register and sign contracts where possible and respect them. A bird ready to sell with no buyer is a bird still eating your feed, and feed is the bulk of your working capital.

history.content: Why look for buyers before I even have birds to sell? Justify.

draws.answer: Because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists the buyers before the farm, and it sets the rule itself: look for them before the batch starts, keep a client register, and sign contracts where you can. Without them you are selling into the flow, which is selling against what you produced. The 2017 ESFT village compendium adds one other reason, without a client you do not have customers to lose. And it puts the money in the money: the same reference says to work out the cost of production per head and to sell above it, so a client is a buyer you can charge.

Because the study gives you a reason that is worth knowing before you open the first henhouse: no bird sells well as a last minute request, and the money depends on the count you set before you set a date. Selling at the wrong time is selling when the flock is small, and a small flock is what the study prices at. The figures it gives for one bird at six months are 1,422 FCFA in one study, and at six months that same bird weighs 1.3 kg, in 2020 prices. So the price you are asking for depends on what you were selling at that moment rather than on the value of the bird. And the whole arrangement is about setting a price from your own recorded losses, not whatever a buyer wants at this moment.

per_item.reference: Check the spacing first, because it is the instruction most often missed: if you put cowpea, groundnut or cassava in with your maize, widen the spacing between the pockets. The brochure says to do it and does not give a reason, but a maize sown at its pure spacing with a second crop between the rows is carrying two crops on one crop's room. Then go through the six things the catalogue asks you to respect when associating: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs, and the period over which the two share the plot. ICAT can look at the plot.

history.content: I put cowpea in with my maize and both did badly.

draws.answer: Do not, and you will lose the rest of the season. That is the instruction in the brochure: use a tolerant variety and sow improved tolerant varieties from ITRA or a registered seed seller, along with the three maize grain protectant and the ash step. Maize is given a different answer, which is to improve the field, clear it, then do better land use, which is to widen the spacing between the pockets. So the problem is with the crop rather than with the varieties. Two things to do next: buy the variety from ITRA or a registered seed seller, because the list is not yours; and ask ICAT where the improved varieties are available.
