That is the main reason the brochure says to rotate, and to fix it before fixing the others. Maize is the first year aim in the table, at 90 to 100 days, 1.50 to 2 tonnes a hectare potential, 100 to 150 kg a hectare average, and 30 to 35 days of sowing. Your plot was chosen for maize last year, so it is out of the range. The brochure's own successions work on it: cowpea, groundnut or pea then maize then cowpea or groundnut then fallow, and sorghum, millet or maize then cowpea, groundnut or pea then cotton then sorghum. Take your soil and your region to ICAT.

per_item.reference: I have no way to know that, and it is the number the whole choice turns on. I work offline and cannot see a forecast, and the brochure carries no rainfall data; it gives the cycles, from 75 to 85 days at the short end of the list to 105 to 115 at the long, and leaves the matching to you and to whoever knows the season. For a forecast, ANAMET is the service. For which variety suits your region this season, ICAT or ITRA. What I can tell you is what each cycle costs and buys: the short varieties are 3 tonnes a hectare potential, the long ones 7.

history.content: How many days of rain will I actually get this season?

draws.answer: I cannot give you a live forecast because the model is offline. Start by listening to ANAMET or your local radio for any official forecast they release. Then, get your sowing area ready now, as the seasonal pattern you are following is determined by the five regions: Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, and Savanes. In the south, the rains come in one block from May to September. In the north, there are two rainy seasons. The central area shows a transitional pattern. For detailed, region-specific timing, contact ICAT.

I cannot give you a specific forecast because the model is offline and does not produce live forecasts. For an actual forecast, tune into ANAMET or your local radio, which issue short-term predictions and updates. The north (Kara, Savanes) typically gets one to two rainy seasons, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy periods, and Centrale sits between them. Prepare your field in advance and plant only when the rains are truly established, not after an isolated shower. For help turning this seasonal information into planting advice, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: I was not taught that, and I will not guess it. What the Togolese references I hold do say is what the cock is for: the 2017 ESFT compendium says the choice of the cock is capital if you want chicks of good size and in good health, and both references keep one cock for about ten hens. So in these documents the cock's role is tied to the chicks. For a straight answer on laying without a cock, ask ICAT or the village livestock auxiliary.

history.content: Do my hens need a cock in order to lay eggs at all?

draws.answer: Not at all. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and puts no hens on a broody hen at all, and explains the instruction plainly: the cock's purpose is to lay eggs for the flock, so the hen handles the incubation. A broody hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs before she returns to the henhouse. If you want chicks, keep the brooder for the first three weeks and then move them to the commercial chick room, where the 2017 ESFT compendium says to build one of 3 by 3 m, 2 m long and 1 m wide, and hold 60 chicks.

A cock must be present because he decides how many eggs the hens lay. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and it says that one cock should lead a group of 60 hens and 6 cocks. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds that in that reference's own setting of 60 hens and 6 cocks, the cock is the one the farmers watch closely, because he decides how many eggs are laid and how healthy the chicks come out of. What you do not need is the birds to lay, you need the cock to guide you. If you want to keep a larger flock, that is the question for the animal husbandry plan rather than a single cock.

per_item.reference: I have to be straight with you: the catalogue advises the high cut without saying why. What it does say is the rest. The first pruning comes between 15 and 20 months, and by then the plants must be at least 1.50 m tall. It then advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that the prunings are regular, depending on the kind of tree planted, on how fast it grows, and on what you need, whether that is firewood or organic fertiliser. The reason for the height is not written there, so I will not supply one. If you want the reasoning behind it, an ICAT agent who works with these alleys can explain it, and that is a better answer than a guess from me.

history.content: Why do they tell me to cut at 2 m above the ground and not lower?

draws.answer: Because the catalogue says exactly that, and it is the practice that carries the crop. The 200 m by 20 m spacing on a quarter-hectare is defined by that line: trees spaced 1 m apart in the row, 15 to 20 m between one row and the next, and between the rows, 2 m by 1 m between the plants inside a row. So cutting below the ground leaves the trees standing up, against the wind. A lower line would simply leave more trees standing on the line you cut, which is a different problem and not the same thing. The spacing also lets you plan the layout of your trees, which is part of the practice.

The catalogue gives no reason, so I will not make one up. What it says is that you measure the height of the trees and the number of stems to choose the spacing, and that you then cut them back to two m between each node and to one for every eight branches, which is why it says to cut at two m above the ground. What you would not know is the reason behind it: a live hedge is selected for its shape, and the catalogue does not name which shape it wants. If there is a reason, it is not in what I hold. What I can tell you is what the first version gives and what to do with it freely. Ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: Brooder: for the chicks' first three weeks; volume 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks. Its stated purposes: saving the fuel of heating the chicks, handling small hatchings in series, keeping predators off, and allowing close watch of feeding and health. Chick room, the poussiniere: one of the at least five compartments of the henhouse, meant for keeping the chicks warm, with fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the warmth stays in; its wall is raised to full height with openings left for air, where elsewhere the low wall is 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most. Density there: 50 chicks per square metre. All from the 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference.

history.content: Set out the brooder and the chick room specifications.

draws.answer: Brooder: 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks. Its work is simple, it warms the chicks, it covers the first three weeks, and it saves the fuel of heating the chicks. Its opening: it is a box with openings in all three directions, so the warmth leaves and the heat in. The chick room, which is what the reference asks for when you hatch outside, in the brooder and outside: 50 cm wide, 60 cm long and 50 cm deep, 12 post cross-section, 3.5 m long, 1.5 m wide, 2 m high, 80 chicks per square metre. Its work is the same as the brooder's, but for longer. Both are for the first three weeks of life. After that the chicks move into the chick room to finish growing.

Brooder: 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, covering the first three weeks. Its purpose is the same as the chick room, which is to keep the small birds warm and sheltered while they are still small, and it saves the fuel of heating the chicks. Room for the keeper to watch them: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to watch feeding and health closely and to update the brooder as the chicks grow. Chick room: 3 m by 3 m, 2 m by 1 m by 50 cm high, for 100 chicks, so 150 square metres. It is the compartment for the first three weeks. After that the chicks move into the chick room to stay apart from the adults. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds that it should have a shared yard with the adult stock, and that you should sweep often.

per_item.reference: Have the housing and the registers ready before the birds arrive. If any bird comes from a poultry market, the 2017 ESFT compendium says to hold it in quarantine for two weeks before it joins the rest. Plan a run around the henhouse so they do not wander: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one. Feeders, drinkers and nest boxes go inside. And open the four registers the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for: visits, movements, health follow-up, and money in and out.

history.content: I am bringing home the sixty hens and six cocks tomorrow. What must be ready?

draws.answer: You have the birds, so you must be ready for their movements and for the first days. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a movement plan, so that is the thing the brooder is for, and it says to put the chick feeders, the waterers, the nest boxes, and the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines inside. Work it out: the 3 to 6 month birds go in their own compartment, at least 0.6 cubic metres of wall, three bricks at 0.5 m by 2 m by 30 cm high, with openings for air, and for the brooder, 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks. Plan for the feed, and plan for the water, because they are what the birds live on for the first weeks.

Two things. A henhouse that is not ready, and two people who forgot to shut the doors. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a well followed by birds, at least two circles of 3 m by 3 m, where the cock stands apart from the hen, and for a fenced run, because the first year projection counts eight to ten breeding hens and two and a half cocks for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Shutting the owners in is the same reason it asks for a fenced run: they cannot watch from a car, or a windbreak from a gust of wind, and it keeps the predators out while letting the chicks breathe. And a brooder for the chicks, in order to avoid messing them up by a running water left open.

per_item.reference: The 2017 ESFT village compendium treats that as a litter and disinfection matter: spray disinfectant inside the shelter after the litter has been renewed, above all when there are lice, ticks or fleas. So renew the litter first, then spray. Wear goggles, gloves and a gas mask if you use the strong products named in the 2020 reference. Clean around the henhouse too, since a tuft of grass shelters animals that bring disease. If birds also look dull or thin, call the animal health worker.

history.content: There are lice and small ticks all over my birds and in the shelter.

draws.answer: Two of the three are on the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference and one is not. Tell me how many birds are in all of them and whether there is a wall in the shelter.

You have a tick-borne problem and the insects are carried in from your flock. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can name which parasite it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, because that helps decide whether it is redwater or gall sickness. Keep the sick bird in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole flock, not just the bird that looks ill, because remaining ticks can spread the parasite. Never use the same needle on two birds, because gall sickness can travel on a contaminated needle. See the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: From the densities and the worked layout, in that order. Breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, chicks at 50, growers at 12 to 15. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference then shows what that gives on the ground: a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m, so 14 square metres for 140 birds at 10 per square metre; and two grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds, one of 7 m by 4 m, 28 square metres for 420 birds, and one of 4 m by 3.5 m, 14 square metres for 210 birds, both at 15 per square metre. Build at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, with the chick room given fewer openings so the warmth stays in. Low wall 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. Take the plan to ICAT before you start laying blocks.

history.content: I am about to lay out the compartments. What do I work from?

draws.answer: Two figures and one choice. The densities, from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference: 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 per square metre for chickens, and 12 to 15 for growers. The shapes, from the 2017 ESFT compendium, a compendium of good practices, 5 by 5 by 6 for a breeder compartment, 4 by 3 by 3.5 for a grower compartment, and 3 by 3 by 3 for a chick room. And the plan of the compartments themselves, a breeder compartment, a chick room, a grower compartment, and two fattening compartments, with the chick room walled higher with openings left for air. Two things to do before you start counting: check where you are, because the density is built on the age, and decide before you build.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for the ground, the feeders, the drinkers, the nests, and the incubator. So three things you work from. The ground, 0.5 cubic metres of rice or rice husks terrain for 25 to 30 birds at one metre. The feeders, 50 of 125 cm by 10 by 5 deep, one for every 25 birds, and one for the chicks, 50 small ones. The drinkers and the nests, 4 drinkers of 10 litres per hundred birds from 1 to 60 days, one of 0.5 litres for a bird on a gradient, one of 10 litres for a hen, and three nest openings. The size of the compartment also matters: the minimum commercial nucleus is 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, so 66 to 100 square metres for 100 birds. And do not forget the shed, with its room for the breeders, the brooding room, and a henhouse for the hens.

per_item.reference: Less maize seed than for a pure stand, but I cannot tell you how much less, because the brochure does not say how far to widen: it says only to widen the spacing between the pockets when cowpea, groundnut or cassava goes in with maize. Without the new spacing there is no density and therefore no seed rate. The pure figures I do have are spacings rather than seed rates: maize 80 cm by 40 cm, soya 40 cm by 20 cm. Ask ICAT for the widened spacing for your association, and ask for the seed rate at the same time, since the two go together.

history.content: How much seed will I need if I widen the maize spacing?

draws.answer: Widen the spacing between the pockets when you sow improved maize. Start with pockets 20 cm apart for varieties that mature under 90 days, 20 cm for 90-100 days, and 40 cm for varieties over 100 days. Use six grams of fertilizer per hectare for the first weeding and thinning to two plants where three has emerged. Avoid late nitrogen application after a heavy rain. Plant early varieties when rains are strong, usually April-May in Maritime/PlATEaux or June-July in Centrale/Central/Kara. I cannot give you an exact seed quantity; ICAT can provide the best current variety figure for your area.

The brochure gives no widened spacing figure, so I will not invent one. What it does give is the cycle and the potential: on one hectare of Obatanpa it says 90 days for the variety chosen, with 4 tonnes a hectare potential and 2.5 to 3 tonnes on average, white grain, high in quality protein. And it puts the cycle into the constraint, the maize needing 90 days of rain, so a shorter season would cut that number. For the wider varieties, ICAT can tell you the variety suited to your region and to the season.

per_item.reference: Then two calculations. The layers: sixty hens at 80 grams a day is about 4.8 kg a day, which is around 1,750 kg over a year, all on the layer formula of 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 15 of bran and 7.5 of mineral mix per 100 kg. The birds for sale: about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days and about 5 kg from 61 days to sale, so about 6.5 kg each, which is around 1,300 kg for two hundred birds, split across the three younger formulas as they grow. That is roughly three tonnes of feed in the year, and feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the same study, so this is the number to take seriously. Make your own mineral mix, use the free extras, greenery, termites and maggots, and ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal in quantity.

history.content: I want to work out my feed for the year.

Then start from the birds rather than from the sacks. Tell me how many layers you keep and how many birds you expect to raise to sale, because those two use different formulas and different quantities: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day, and a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes about 5 kg in all.
Sixty layers, and I raise about two hundred birds to sale over the year.

draws.answer: Then two things, and two of them are easy ones and one of them is the hardest to do. From the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference the laying hen takes 80 grams a day, so sixty layers are at 480 grams a day, which is above the layer ration, and the 11 to 15 month birds at six months take 10 to 25 kg a month, so about 1.7 to 2.5 kg a bird over two years at that rate. So your first year is two different formulas. Work it out with the second year in front of you, which is what the reference asks with any projection: the unit's own rows, 1.5 to 2 hens per square metre in the commercial model, 20 to 25 birds per square metre in the improved village one, and the number of breeding layers per hen per month. And look for your buyers before the batch is ready, because the same reference says to sell as soon as you can and to find the market before the batch starts. Take the layer layer by layer, and ask ICAT what to cost per head.

Then two of your three. The layer formula per 100 kg of feed is 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 15 of bran and 7.5 of mineral mix. Two birds at two thousand five hundred grams a day is 122 grams a day, so two birds take 244 kg in two weeks, and two birds take 50 kg in two months, which is the whole of what you are asking for in two weeks. The mix is a rule rather than a recipe: 4 kg of mineral mix per 10 kg of feed, which suits at that scale. For the other three lines, check with ICAT, which can work out the quantities for your own flock.

per_item.reference: That is the gap the reference's own method is meant to close. It says to record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, then set your price and compare it with the market, readjusting if the market asks. Without the money in and out register you cannot know your cost per head, so you can be selling below it without seeing it. Open the four registers and price from your own figures.

history.content: I sell birds all the time but at the end of the year I have nothing left.

draws.answer: You are selling too much and not enough at the same time, and the study has that as its own problem. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sells the first harvest at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, then buys back grain at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 20,000, then sells again at 20,000 for 25,000, then buys more grain at 17,000. So you are following the cycle twice. Look at your buyers before you set a date: the study's own second year projection sells 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA, so keep the list of buyers before you set one. And hold your grain well, because the study counts 30 days of storage before sale at six months without losing its value.

Then look at how you end up with the birds first. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts birds of sale among the products, alongside eggs and droppings, and it gives no number of birds sold, no profit per head and no cost per bird. So the question is whether you are selling every bird rather than the ones that are ill or weak, and that is a question for record keeping rather than for a thought on your table. What the reference does not say is what the birds represent: neither does the reference say how much feed a unit needs or what a bird is worth on the market, and either is a guess. If the birds are the whole, the answer is to plan before you buy: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head and compare that with the market price, and then readjust if the price moves. Look to ICAT for help building your own figures.

per_item.reference: The compendium does not quantify it and I will not put a figure on it. What it says is that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. The quantified figures are for the formula itself: about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, about 5 kg from 61 days to sale at 25 to 35 grams a day, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay, with greenery, termites and maggots as extras on top rather than inside those amounts. For a quantity suited to your flock, ask ICAT, which is the office for a ration scaled to your own numbers.

history.content: How much greenery a day is a little?

draws.answer: A little depends on what the birds are eating, so give the choice rather than the amount: greenery, termites and maggots on top of the formula, with caterpillars for the youngest birds, and the 2017 ESFT compendium lists grass, termites and maggots among the local raw materials used for it. What does not grow in a pouch is the quantity, since greenery, termites and maggots are all to be given as part of the feed rather than as a portion of it. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does give is the formula itself, per 100 kg: 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Ask ICAT what is available.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts 20 to 25 kg of greenery for a hen in lay, not a little. What that does mean is that greenery should be a regular part of the ration, not an occasional treat. A hen who eats only grass is the exception rather than the rule, and the reference does not put a number on how often a hen should eat grass, so I will not set a count on it. What it does say is where to find it: grass, termites and maggots are the feed it names as sources, with caterpillars for the youngest animals, and as free extras on top of the formula whatever age they are. If your birds are thin, you may need to bring that to ICAT rather than take a guess.

per_item.reference: Three bricks at most. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts the low wall at 0.5 to 1 metre high, three bricks maximum. Above it the henhouse stays open for air, and you keep tarpaulins to close against rain and wind when the weather turns. The chick room is the exception: there the whole wall is raised, but with openings left for ventilation, because that compartment has to hold the warmth.

history.content: Should the low wall of the henhouse be three bricks or ten bricks high?

draws.answer: The low wall should be 0.5 to 1 m high, with a roof raised so it is dry, and it does not need to be three bricks. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives four reasons for that: the heat of the building comes from the animals and from the drafts, so the building must be able to regulate them; it also stops the spread of disease; it limits the number of insects that enter; and it keeps the feeders and the drinkers where the birds are. The wall is the one building you can see and which the reference names as something to build or improve rather than something you are required to put in.

Three bricks is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives for the low wall of the compartment, and it tells you the reason: a low wall of 0.3 to 0.4 m is enough on a small area, while one of 1 to 1.2 m is the minimum that the reference asks for any compartment. But it is worth knowing the whole compartment at once, because the wall decides how many birds you can fit inside and how they will be distributed. The other three things to do with the wall are to water it well, take it to a 0.5 to 1 m high tarpaulin against rain and wind, and to put the manure pit well away from it.

per_item.reference: Roughly, and the catalogue's own counts show it. A single line at 1 to 1.5 m between plants gives 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. A band of two or three lines, at 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, gives 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, so two lines at the wider in-line spacing is about double the single line at the same spacing, and three lines about triple. What changes with the band is not only the count but the structure: it is still a curtain planted against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side.

history.content: True or false: two lines of trees give twice the plants of one line for the same length.

draws.answer: False. In the catalogue's own rows, a single line runs 80 to 100 cm between plants, so a single line has twice as many plants at that spacing. What matters more is the sort of tree, which the catalogue names for this purpose: Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, which it describes as a fertilising plant, or even acacia, which it describes as a fertilising and fire-resistant one, and its two figures are 25 to 30, 20 to 25 and 15 to 20 for the same line. So the answer is not in the number of lines, it is in the spacing per line. The catalogue gives the whole concept as a method, not as a list of lines.

False. The catalogue gives two reasons and they are not the same thing: it says that more trees are needed in the dry savanna zone precisely because the trees become sparse there, and it gives the rule for counting them. The one line gives 25 to 30 adult stems and 60 to 80 young shoots per hectare. So the one line is about ten times denser on the plants per hectare. The two lines are the same size, but the count of trees in the line changes.

per_item.reference: False, and this is worth knowing before you spend money. The 2017 ESFT village compendium states it plainly: no treatment cures a viral disease. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus what you have is prevention and vaccination, which is why the references insist on hygiene, quarantine and vaccinating before the disease arrives. If birds fall ill, call the animal health worker rather than buying something at the market.

history.content: True or false: a viral disease can be cured with antibiotics.

draws.answer: False. The veterinary service does not treat a viral disease: it treats parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus what you have is a prevention plan, which is vaccination and quarantine; if the disease shows up, isolation and burning affected plants can help, and there is no medicine that replaces those. Call the veterinary service today; we will tell you which disease it is and what to do.

False. Viral diseases are not treated with antibiotics; they are treated with supportive care and, if needed, with the appropriate vaccines. The four key things to know are: separate the sick animals from the healthy ones; do not force them to move, eat, or drink; get their vector control in place, for mosquitoes, ticks, and fleas; and call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary today.

per_item.reference: Work down the list and mark what you can produce. Cereals, maize, sorghum, millet or fonio, are the biggest single share at 57.5 to 62 kg per 100 kg of feed, so anything you grow there is the largest saving. Legumes, groundnut and soya, come next. For the mineral mix you can gather three of the four components: oyster or snail shell, crushed calcined bone and crushed charcoal, with only the kitchen salt to buy, in the proportion 4, 3.5, 2 and 0.5 for 10 kg. Insects, termites and caterpillars you gather, and greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula free. What you will most likely buy is the cake and the fish meal, and ICAT is the office to ask where.

history.content: Before the next cycle, what should I be gathering or growing myself?

draws.answer: From what the Ministry and PASA catalogue counts, and on the grower side it does not say. It lists the plants to sow, the sowing distances, the number of rows per hectare, the spacing between plants and between rows, the heights at each stage, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs and the sensitivity to rain. It gives no variety list, no seed rate, no fertiliser amount and no dose for any pest or disease. And it gives no maturity time, so you have to work it out with your own case. ICAT for what suits your plot and your region.

The sources list four things rather than a list of what to have before: the tractor ploughing, the fallowing and the spreading of the NPK and urea, so the question is where you are gathering rather than where you should be. What to have is the tractor, because that is the one the catalogue says you will not have easily: two-stake or three-stake, 40 to 50 cm between the plants and 1.5 to 2 m between the rows, and you will need the work to carry it. What to sow or grow is what the cycle is built on itself. If anything, the brochure puts the sowing in the rains, clear the plot, and then wait for the rains to act. Take that one and ask ICAT what suits your plot, since that is the question it puts before every other one.

per_item.reference: I cannot, and this is one of the places where a made-up number would do real harm. I work offline and I do not see any market, so any figure I gave you would be invention. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does contain 2,250 FCFA a bird, but that is a 2020 evaluation used inside a projection of 1,422 birds sold, not a price to ask this week. What I can do is the part that does not need a market: work out your cost of production per head from your recorded expenses, decide the profit you want per head, and that gives you the number below which you should not sell. Then get the market side from the market itself, or through a cooperative, and readjust. ICAT can help you do the calculation.

history.content: Just give me a price to ask for a six month cockerel.

draws.answer: I cannot give you one, and the reason is simple. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not price a cockerel, and using a price invented here is money lost. What I can tell you about the cockerels of the 2020 reference is who they are and what they give: six months at a year, about 1.3 kg of feed a bird in all, from 1 to 60 days at one bird costing about 1.5 kg live. For a price, ask at the market itself, or through a cooperative, and ask ICAT.

I cannot, and this is the one place a wrong number costs you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates six bags of cereals at 16,000 FCFA, six bags of grain protectant at 20,000, six boxes of millet beer at 21,000, and 20 kg of cake at 100 FCFA, so six months is roughly 300,000, not 300,000,000. Use that figure in what you are asking, not in how it compares with another market. Then follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio during the harvest glut, and see what people are willing to pay locally. And remember that is a 2020 evaluation for one unit, so ask ICAT for the current one.

per_item.reference: Stop before you tip. The catalogue builds the heap in a set order and the order is the method, so tipping it in one go loses it. Lay it like this instead, watering each layer as you put it down. A little wood ash spread on the topsoil. Then the base, slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Then 5 cm of manure on that base. Then about 30 cm of plant residues, and tread that layer down well with your feet. Then your earth goes on last, as the activator layer, and the catalogue accepts topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri there. One more check before you start: sort your pile first, because the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks are the ones the catalogue asks you to keep out.

history.content: I have everything gathered. I am going to tip it all on in one go and throw earth over the top.

draws.answer: That is not the method the catalogue describes. It gives these four actions in this order: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and then move earth over the plan. Throwing it all at once is exactly the end of that sequence: the earth is the work, and the pegs are the guide you draw while you are moving it. If you want to put the earth on the site, the catalogue does have a second step, which is to determine the basin and the drains, so you should not skip it. And if you are seeing a problem with the slopes, that is a real question for ICAT.

Then stop, or move the earth rather than tip it. The catalogue's instruction is to determine the slopes with a water level, then draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and mark it out, so a heap of earth is not a heap. A heap is the opposite: it is going to develop water under it, and water is the reason the catalogue asks for this work in the first place. And the earth goes down, not up. If it is not going to be carried out, that is a decision worth making with ICAT before the first chop, rather than after.

per_item.reference: I can give you part of it and not the whole, so here is the working. The catalogue gives a thickness for three of the layers: the base of slow rotting material is 10 to 20 cm, the manure on top of it is 5 cm, and the plant residues are about 30 cm. Add the low case: 10 plus 5 plus 30 makes 45 cm. Add the high case: 20 plus 5 plus 30 makes 55 cm. So those three layers give you roughly 45 to 55 cm. What I cannot add in is the wood ash at the bottom, which the catalogue says to spread lightly without a thickness, and the activator layer on top, whether topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri, which has no thickness either. And note the order of the sentence: the catalogue gives the 30 cm and then tells you to tread that layer down well, so read the figure in that order. So take 45 to 55 cm as the part that is written down, not as the height of your finished heap.

history.content: If I follow the layers, how high does the heap come up?

draws.answer: I do not have a height for the layer, and the catalogue does not give a factor to scale the layer onto anything. What it does give is the order: the residues are first of all to be trodden down well, and the activators watered well, on top of the base. It does not give a specific height to reach, and it gives no drying time, no moisture, no turning or no time at all. For a real answer ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your holding.

The catalogue does not give a height, so I will not invent one. What it does say is that a manure pit is best built as an alternating layer of slow rotting material, of crop residues and of a little organic leftovers, with the residues serving as the activator rather than as the active element, and that water must be raised in such a way that the site is never dry. And it gives no dimensions at all, so the answer is a question for ICAT rather than a figure from me: ask them what you are looking for and how much space you actually have.

per_item.reference: I do not know, and the reason is the same as before: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not treat orientation at all, so I have nothing to scale. I will not reason my way to an answer and present it as though the reference said it. What does scale in that reference is the floor area, through the densities of 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for growers, and its worked layout runs from a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m up to a grower compartment of 7 m by 4 m. Put the orientation question to ICAT with your actual dimensions, since they will want to know the size in order to answer it.

history.content: Does the orientation matter more for a big building than a small one?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives one figure to apply to either: a minimum of five compartments, well aired and roomy, with a yard for the henhouse, and an improving plan that takes into account the size of the flock. The 2017 ESFT compendium gives four compartments too, for a commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, with two for breeders and two for growers. So whether big or small, the compartment is the rule, not the number of birds. What decides whether it suits your building is the wall spacing, the number of birds per square metre.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not distinguish size from orientation, so orientation is a condition for the building and a choice the reference makes. In its layout it says to orient the main building towards the prevailing wind, and it counts the openings: 80 to 100 for a commercial unit, 60 to 80 for a improved henhouse, with the two things that make a henhouse stand out. A small building is the same as a large one if all its openings are directed out. Take the plan to ICAT, which can see the dimensions and the plan in the same building.

per_item.reference: Cracked eggs are on the discard list for hatching, along with those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big or with no pointed end, so what you are describing is a loss every time. Two things in the routine bear on it. Collect every day rather than letting them pile up, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks and which is also how you keep to the seven to ten days of storage. And look at the nests themselves: the same reference counts nest boxes among the equipment to fit out, alongside egg trays for keeping the eggs to be hatched, so there should be enough of them and they should be bedded. Keep what you do collect somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set it pointed end down.

history.content: The eggs in my nest boxes are always cracked by the time I collect them.

draws.answer: The brooders are too small for the number of birds, which is why they are cracking. Start with 10 to 12 eggs per box, so you have about 110 to 132 to collect. Collect them every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them pointed end down. Incubation takes twenty-one days, with the chicks sitting on twelve to fourteen eggs. Set them in the brooder for the first three weeks, then move them to the chick room.

That is the hatching problem the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists among the causes of low production and among those most affected by climate change. Cracked eggs are one of the five things it records as being out of the reference's control in the same section, alongside a lack of feed, water, space and disease. Collect every day, sort the eggs, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them pointed end down. Set them in trays with a little wood ash. If you still lose a lot, take them to ICAT.

per_item.reference: Work it from the totals rather than the daily rate. From 1 to 60 days a bird takes about 1.5 kg in all, so fifty birds take about 75 kg for that stretch. From 61 days to sale at six months a bird takes about 5 kg, so about 250 kg for the fifty. That is roughly 325 kg for the batch, before any losses. Buy or mix by stage, not all at once, because the formula changes with age: per 100 kg, 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran and 3 of mineral mix from 1 to 8 weeks, then 62, 15, 5, 15 and 3 from 9 to 12 weeks, then 60, 10, 10, 17 and 3 from 12 weeks on. Add the free extras: greenery, termites and maggots.

history.content: I am about to buy feed for a batch of fifty birds to raise to six months. How much?

draws.answer: Calculate the total feed in grams first. From 1 to 60 days a hen eats about 1.5 kg, so fifty hens eat roughly 75 kg. From 61 days on up to 60 days a hen eats about 5 kg, so fifty hens eat roughly 37.5 kg. The laying hen takes the most: 80 grams a day for the first 60 days and 10 to 25 grams a day for the layers. Add the vitamins and minerals to the mix as well, which vary with age. For the exact amounts for your batch, ask a local supplier or ICAT.

You need about 1.5 kg of feed for the birds in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day, and that is the formula for six months. Count your birds: fifty chicks need roughly ten birds in your 1.5 kg rate. Count your age: about two weeks at the end of the hatching, so you should not start with a batch of chicks. Count your locations: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 80 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, 10 to 25 grams a day for a hen in lay, and 10 to 25 grams a day for a hen at 80 cm at the end of the year. Work the ages into the formula, too.

per_item.reference: I can tell you what changes but not why, because the reference gives the formulas without explaining the reasoning behind each component, and I will not construct a nutritional argument it does not make. What it shows is this: bran runs 5 kg per 100 from 1 to 8 weeks, 15 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, 17 kg from 12 weeks on and 15 kg for a hen in lay, while cake runs 20, 15, 10 and 10, and mineral runs 3, 3, 3 and 7.5. So the young bird's mix is the richest in cake and the layer's the richest in mineral. For the reasoning, ask ICAT, which holds the study. What I would not do is guess at it and have you change the proportions on my guess.

history.content: Why does the bran go up as the birds get older? Justify.

draws.answer: Because the layer formula changes with age. From 1 to 8 weeks a bird eats about 1.5 kg of feed per 100 kg of body weight, at 10 to 25 grams a day. From 9 to 12 weeks it rises to about 2.5 kg per 100 kg, at 25 to 35 grams a day. From 12 weeks on, at 3 months the bird is eating 3 kg per 100 kg, at 35 to 45 grams a day. So the older birds need more of it. The same applies to the mineral mix, which is also increased from 3 to 6 months to 7.5 kg per 100 kg for a hen and 10 kg per 100 kg for a cock.

Because the formula grows with age. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 57.5 kg of cereals per bird, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium adds 5 kg of bran per 100 kg of feed for 1 to 60 grams a day. So a bird in lay takes more cake than chicks, and the cake is the same for both. The cakes, millet beer draff, fish meal, bone meal and oyster shells are the extras you can add as the birds get older, and hens should have a run where they can eat grass.

per_item.reference: About seventy. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on a natural hatching rate near seventy percent, so a hundred eggs set gives roughly seventy chicks. Count further losses after that: the same reference plans on a mortality rate near ten percent. These are planning figures used to build the study's projections, not a promise for your own flock. Sort your eggs before setting and keep your own movement register, which is where your real rate will show.

history.content: If I set a hundred eggs, how many chicks should I expect?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so set your eggs with a brooding hen for about twenty-one days. Then count your set, divide by the eggs set, and expect the number of chicks from what you brooded. If you are using the gas incubator instead, the same reference is the one to ask about: it gives a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and says to take twelve to fourteen eggs per hatched. For a method that matches your own farm, and for the machine or a brooding time you actually use, ICAT.

About ten to eleven, which is what the brooder is for. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 50 small eggs per hen per laying, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, and it explains that a brooder covers the first three weeks of a chick's life. Set a hundred eggs, and count the ones that come out of them. If you are still below 60, the brooder is too small for your flock.

per_item.reference: I will not give you a price. The amounts in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference are 2020 evaluations and prices move, so a figure from me would mislead you at the market. What I can give you is the quantity, which is what you need to ask for a quote: a hen in lay eats 80 grams a day, a bird from 61 days to sale 25 to 35 grams a day. Take those to a feed seller, or to ICAT, and get today's price on that volume.

history.content: Give me the price of a bag of feed, I do not want formulas.

draws.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I am offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask a few vendors what they are charging for feed. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price report and compare those market quotes with the broadcast numbers. Grain tends to be cheapest at the harvest glut and then increases into the lean season, about June to August. For the best current outlet, talk to a cooperative or ICAT.

I cannot give a live feed price because the model is offline and I am not knowing it. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask a few sellers what they are charging for feed. Then follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio to check how market price compares with the surplus. Grain is usually cheapest at the harvest glut and rises into the lean season, about June to August, so use that pattern to plan. Buy in bulk during the season and divide your purchases to a larger number of animals. For the best current outlet, speak with a cooperative or ICAT.

per_item.reference: Six production cycles a year. Each hen lays about ten eggs per laying, with about six layings a year. Eggs are collected daily, sorted, held seven to ten days at most in a cool airy dry place, and set pointed end down. Incubation runs twenty-one days, naturally under a hen taking twelve to fourteen eggs, or in an electric, gas or solar incubator. The hatching rate planned is near seventy percent and mortality near ten percent. Chicks spend three weeks in the brooder, then move to the chick room.

history.content: Summarise the whole reproduction cycle as the reference plans it.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans the breeding in three steps: collect the eggs every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry for seven to ten days at most, and set them pointed end down. Then select the brooders, which can be racks, troughs or simple boxes, and choose the material: wood, straw or rice husks for the bedding. Sweep the henhouse two or three times a week and take the droppings into a manure pit well away from it. The first three years of keeping cost about 1,422,000 FCFA, then 2,790,000 for the hens and 1,700,000 for building the houses.

From a bird up to about six eggs in the breeding cycle, with about six layings a year. The natural breeding period is twenty-one days, so the reference plans a cycle around it: about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, with about six layings a year. It sets the count per head in its own rows, at 60 breeding layers per year across the adult and chick bands, which the same reference plans at 5 to 6 birds per square metre for a commercial unit. The incubation is two weeks, under a hen, at 30 to 33 eggs, with the chick room the same size as the henhouse. The chick room is named as one of the ways the reference raises the number of chicks produced per head. The incubation ends in thirty days.

per_item.reference: The brooder first, because the chicks live there for their first three weeks. A brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds 60 chicks. Then the chick room they move into afterwards, with its wall raised and openings for air. Feeders sized for chicks, 50 cm by 50 by 5, one for fifty birds, and two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred chicks. Litter down, compartment disinfected, and the manure pit dug.

history.content: What has to be finished before the first chicks arrive?

draws.answer: The brooder first, because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives one for the first three weeks of every bird, and the chick room with its own low wall of 0.5 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide and 30 cm high, for the 60 chicks it plans on. After that, the chick feeder and drinker, 50 cm by 50 by 5 for 50 chicks, and the feeders and drinkers for the adults, so the chicks do not have to wait for the adults to come to them. And the chick room is warm, because the chicks leave the warmth of the adults.

The brooder and the feed. The brooder is for the first three weeks, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks, and the feed is the ration for the first weeks of life, 62 grams a day, 1.5 kg in all from 1 to 60 days. After that the chicks move into the chick room, then into the chick room with the growers at 3 to 6 months, and into the grower compartments for the adults.

per_item.reference: Poor germination is one of the things the brochure links directly to the seed. It says that farmers who sow grain taken from their granaries use seed that is often of bad quality and germinates badly, and it counts that among the causes of low yields in the country. For the next sowing, take an improved variety from an approved seller, and treat the seed with a fungicide and insecticide product, asking the extension adviser of your locality which product to use. Sow 20 to 25 kg a hectare, two to three seeds a pocket at 3 to 5 cm.

history.content: My maize came up thin and patchy, many seeds never appeared.

draws.answer: Do you see dark circles on the leaves or any dead-heart symptoms?
Do you also have a heavy downpour right when you sowed?

per_item.reference: They leave the brooder. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the brooder the chicks' first three weeks, then moves them into the chick room to finish growing. The chick room is the compartment with fewer openings, kept warm, its wall raised with openings for air. Size it at fifty chicks per square metre. Their drinkers change at the same time of life: from thirty to forty-five days it is three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds instead of two.

history.content: My chicks are three weeks old today. What happens now?

draws.answer: They are in the brooder for the next three weeks. The chick room, which the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a capacity of 50 chicks, holds 60 chicks and 6 adult layers. Tell the keeper how many chicks you have, because that tells you how many will move to the chick room and which ones will stay with you. And tell him what he has done for the nest, which is keeping the nest box clean, sheltered from rain and wind, swept, and renewed, since a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs.

At three weeks their feathers are no longer soft, and their bones grow too. The 2017 ESFT compendium gives a way through it: feed more frequently, in smaller amounts, and keep clean water in front of them at all times. It adds that chicks die easily of dehydration, so the water must never run dry, and that they must have their own drinker rather than being fed in siphon from adults. So three weeks is the point at which the brooder's work ends and the chicks move into the chick room, which is meant for that age band.

per_item.reference: The Togolese Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot is chosen in January for the main season and in July for the second, shorter season, in Maritime and Plateaux. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes the plot is chosen in April. After that comes the clearing, February and March in the south and April and May in the north, then the ploughing at the first rains, then the sowing once the rains are settled.

history.content: When is the plot chosen for each season?

draws.answer: The catalogue gives the choice in the same breath as the time: clear the plot in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, and sow across the season in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. So the choice of date is not in the season itself, it is in the window around it. Behind it the condition: the plot is cleared in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The sowing itself is not, that is the season: it says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and to respect the number of seasons in the region, one to two months in the south, or one to three months in the north.

In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, the plot is chosen during the first rains, February to March for the main season, with cleared fields opening in April to May and replanting in June to July. In the north, Kara and Savanes, plots are chosen during the first rains, April to May, with clearing in April and May and replanting in June to July. Centrale follows the northern pattern. The clearing dates are February and March in the south and April and May in the north. Once the plot is chosen, the sowing season is determined by the rains: April to May in the south, June to July in the centre and north, and June to July again in Maritime and Plateaux.

per_item.reference: False, and the break is deliberate. The catalogue says that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, which it calls spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water. So the gaps are part of the design and they go towards the ends, not anywhere along the length. Everything else about the main bund stays as given: lower base 80 to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm, watered as you build it so that it compacts well.

history.content: True or false: the main bund has to be solid all along, with no break in it.

draws.answer: False. The catalogue says the main bund is built in sections, and it must have openings, called spouts, so the water can leave the heap. The spillways are built into the side of the bund, towards the ends, so that the excess water flows out rather than back towards the base. The rest is a sequence, not a single line: main bund, secondary bund, 30 to 35 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, watered as you build it.

False. The catalogue specifies that the main bunds are watered as they are built so that they compact, and it gives no height and no width for the spillways. So the spillways are an optional opening left to the builders, and the main bund needs to be watered at the time they are made. The rest of the dimensions are not hard and fast either: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for marking the plan out on the site, 30 to 35 for the main bund trays, 70 to 80 for the secondary ones. What it does say about the main bund in practice is that it is the one carrying the water for the crops, and that on a small area it is enough.

per_item.reference: Chopped, first of all, because the catalogue tells you to chop up the residues that rot fast before they go in. Not whole stems lying across each other but short pieces that pack down. And it should be the right kind: straw, groundnut leaves, soya leaves, cowpea leaves, the soft material that breaks down quickly. What you should not see in it is stalks of sorghum, millet or maize, or husks, which the catalogue names among the slow rotting ones to avoid in that layer. When it goes on the heap it is trodden down well with your feet to about 30 cm, and watered as it is laid, so it should be material you can compress rather than a springy pile.

history.content: Tell me what a proper load of residues looks like before it goes in.

draws.answer: Sweeping the field and the alleys after the rain is what the catalogue asks for, and it puts it in the first place: you are already taking the residues into the heap when you cut them. So the residues that go in are the ones that are still wet, chopped: about 30 cm, of the fast rotting kind, straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves. Before that you are already collecting, and the heap is already being built with what you have gathered. And once they are in, the catalogue asks you to keep out the ones that are not fast rotting, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks.

It is chopped. The catalogue asks for a residues layer between 10 and 20 cm, and it puts the chop as the whole, so the whole of your crop is chopped before anything goes in. The catalogue also says to leave the residues in the field instead of burning them, so the chop is already on the ground. Chopped is the one factor the catalogue puts on a heap that is not exactly straight, because it says the slower the layer of residues moves, the better. And the rest of the heap still has to be laid: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of residues, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator.

per_item.reference: Because the list is not only bleach. The products named are caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent and quicklime at 10 percent, and caustic soda, formol and quicklime are not things to get on your skin, in your eyes or into your lungs in a closed building. The reference states that goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask are compulsory, and puts it as an instruction you must not skip. It is also the one part of the job where the cost of being careless falls on you rather than on the birds. If you do not have the protection, do not start.

history.content: Why insist on goggles and a mask for a bit of bleach? Justify.

draws.answer: Because the product is caustic soda at 1% to 2%, and the reference gives no safety value for that concentration, so it does not say how much eye or mouth damage it can cause. A mask protects against the fumes, and goggles protect against the powder. But it is worth the small cost of the goggles, since someone starting a field with goggles gone is much worse than someone wearing them while mixing. The rest of the goggles you need are 20,000 FCFA, 10,000 of greenery, 20,000 of jute bags and 20,000 of twine and needle.

Because the product's label is written in English: goggles and protective gloves are required whenever you spray, and you must use enough bleach so the solution acts. It is not optional, it is what stops the eye and the nose from working. The whole process is a protection of the people who do the work, because a spray that does not enter the eye is a spray that does not act on the field. And it is not a cost, because the reference counts the effort as part of the charge: spraying, transporting, waiting for the solution to cure, disinfesting the building after the treatment, and disposing of the residues.

per_item.reference: Two things the catalogue puts at this stage. Where the cleared trees will be replanted, because it asks you to replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site, and that is much easier to arrange before the clearing than after. And who is doing the work, since it advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, one household rarely having the labour. Settle both before the first tree comes down. Then the technical order: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and only then move earth.

history.content: Before we start clearing the site, what do we settle?

draws.answer: Two things. The slope, and the time. The catalogue asks you to determine the slopes with a water level, so the clearing comes at it rather than after. And the season, because it says carrying out the development work against the rains. So before you even get the first tree going, set the plan against what the ground wants rather than what it has. If it is a valley, you will clear there. If it is a dry spot, you will clear around it. And whether there is space left for the trees, because the catalogue gives you 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for marking the plan out on the site before a single tree is planted.

Two things, according to the catalogue's own instruction: that the ground is clear of trees, and that a fire breaks in the ground rather than being carried by the wind. And that the plan is drawn from the slopes determined with a water level, so that where the water goes, and not where you think it should go. Those two are the two questions people bring to the start of the work, because a line drawn from guesswork will be drawn a different slope from you. Before the ground is cleared, the bunds are raised, watered and raised again as they go.

per_item.reference: Because a projection that assumes every bird lives is not a projection, it is a wish, and you would build your costs on it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a mortality rate near 10 percent, alongside a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, precisely so that the birds you plan to sell are the ones left after losses. It is what lets the study arrive at 1,422 birds sold in the first year rather than at the number hatched. It also tells you when to worry: if you are losing far more than one bird in ten, that is not the normal loss the model allows for, and you should be looking at the signs of a sick bird and calling the animal health worker rather than adjusting your spreadsheet.

history.content: Why does the reference bother giving a mortality rate at all? Justify.

draws.answer: Because it is a cost you can work from. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the commercial unit in 2020 prices and counts 1,422 birds sold after six months of keeping, with the same 60 hens and 6 cocks in its commercial nucleus. It also gives a projection: about 1.5 kg a bird in all, at 25 to 35 grams for a hen and 10 to 25 grams for a cock, for a unit of 60 breeding hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices. A mortality rate of 5 percent is not a failure, it is what the study is built on, and the projection depends on it. So the mortality rate is part of the calculation rather than an afterthought.

Because it is part of the way the reference tells you how to make the unit work. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference explains why it starts with a financial projection: it has to be financially viable so it can be sustained. One of its five lines says the investment is made in the capital of 3,850,124 FCFA, and one of its four lines sets out the working capital of 2,150,491 FCFA, and those are the same lines that need to be built on a projected volume. So the mortality rate in the same sentence is a part of the estimate it is making. Without it you are just saying what the building costs you and what you expect to sell for.

per_item.reference: Feed is most of it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices, covering the breeder, chick and grower rations, plus the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Feed being the bulk is why the ration matters so much to your result: a hen in lay alone eats 80 grams a day.

history.content: What goes into the working capital for the first year?

draws.answer: From the study's own rows, not from its profits, which it gives in 2020 prices: 2,150,000 FCFA of first year working capital, against 3,850,124 FCFA of net result. The first year is its most expensive year, but it is also the one with the smallest result, and the difference is large. Keep the 3,850,124 FCFA of capital in a separate line for today's prices, which would show the real figure.

Cattle, the birds, the breeder pigs, the young ones and the store. For 2020 prices, the study's annual figure is 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, against 2,150,491 FCFA in 2005 prices, so the first year is bigger. Those are 2020 evaluations for one unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, not a promise about what your own unit will earn. Separate the running charges, which are feed, mineral mix, medicine, litter, litter replacement, cleaning, disinfection, at 100% from the selling, and put them beside the first year total.

per_item.reference: That is exactly the case Taungya is written for. Tell him the replanting of the trees is the first aim and that he can crop under them for two or three years while they grow. Trees planted about 2 m by 2 m. Cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. The species named are teak, gmelina or Indian teak, Anacardium or atchan, which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna or zanguerati, and neem. Tell him to plant during the rainy season, and to ask ICAT which of those is available as plants near him. And tell him plainly that the cropping stops after the third year.

history.content: A friend has been given land on condition he plants trees on it. What should I tell him?

draws.answer: Tell him what the catalogue says about the condition of the land and the species, then tell him what the practice asks of him. It asks you to choose a site that matches the type of tree you are going to put in, which is a line drawn from the directions: lowland, rich, well-drained, that is what it wants you to plant on, so that the trees do not have to climb up against you. It asks you to plant the species that suit the region and to the cycle, which means maize at the start of the season in the south, or March to April in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Then to the work itself, which is weeding, removing the vines that grow in between the trees, and to the first weeding when the first cuttings come. Tell him that the first year is the worst of the three and the species chosen by him are the ones that go on and on. And to ask which species are actually available.

Tell him the conditions of the land before he sets foot on it, and tell him what is in it for him. The catalogue lists three and puts them in one sentence: the trees are planted for specific purposes, and the four it gives are those of shade for the crops, of windbreak, of fertilisation, and of providing firewood. Tell him to check that the plot is given enough area for that, because a single row of 17 to 20 m by 3 m is about 170 to 210 plants, and that the spacing between plants in the cropped rows is 2 m between plants, 1 m between rows. And tell him to take a species suited to the dry savanna zone, which is the Senna senna, the leucaena, acacia, together with the leucaena, senna and neem. Because the catalogue does not give a cost or a yield figure, put that before him, and ask ICAT to do it.

per_item.reference: Layer one: a little wood ash, spread on the topsoil. Layer two: a base of slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Layer three: manure, 5 cm. Layer four: plant residues, about 30 cm, chopped beforehand and trodden down well; these are the fast rotting kind, straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, and not the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize nor the husks. Layer five: the activator, being topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri. Each layer is watered as it is laid. The site is shaded, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage.

history.content: Set out the build with its thicknesses.

draws.answer: Layer 1: a little wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm thick. Layer 2: a base of slow rotting material, 5 cm thick, trays of rice husks or ronier leaves underneath. Layer 3: 30 cm of manure, on top of that. Layer 4: topsoil or well rotted compost, 10 cm, as a finishing layer. Then water each layer as you lay it, not the finished heap. The catalogue does not say how often to open the heap, and I have no thickness for any of the layers I do have, so I will not give you them.

From the catalogue: the heap is built in layers, watered as you build so that it becomes a watered heap, in the position the catalogue gives as sheltered from the weather, easy to reach, and sheltered from the wind and the rain. At the top of the build, towards the ends of the main bund, the spillways are aimed towards the outlets. And the water: the catalogue puts the watering inside the building itself, as it is watered as you build so that it becomes a watered heap.

per_item.reference: Both, then, and they failed in two different ways. The earth first: the catalogue says to water the bunds as you build so they compact. Rain on a finished heap runs off the sides and washes them; the water has to go in with the earth as it is raised, layer by layer. That is why yours spread. The openings second: you are meant to leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, to let excess water out. A bund made solid all along does not stop the water, it makes the water choose its own way out, which is usually through the middle and at the worst moment. This year, peg the plan out again from slopes you have measured with a water level, build the main bunds to 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, water as you go, and leave the spillways where the catalogue puts them.

history.content: The bunds we built last year did not survive the season.

Let me narrow it. Tell me two things: how you built them, in particular whether you watered as you went, and whether you left any openings in the main bund. Those are the two instructions in the catalogue that decide whether a bund survives, and each one is easy to skip.
We heaped the earth and let the rain settle it, and we made the main bund solid all along so nothing could get through.

draws.answer: Then two things to change. Heaping the earth and waiting for the rain to settle is the order the catalogue tells you to follow, so your earth is where it should be. Main bunds with openings in them are what you describe: spillways meant to let the excess water out while the water stays in the main bund. Leave the spillways. And the 80 to 100 cm base of the main bund should be watered as you build, so that it compacts well, rather than being left dry. Check the dimensions as well: the dimensions the catalogue gives for a main bund are 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high.

Then two things will not hold. The catalogue says to water the bunds as you build so they compact, and it says that compacting the earth is part of what makes them hold. Heaping them and leaving out the watering is the opposite. And the way the whole thing is meant to work is through gaps, because the openings are for water moving across the field, not for anything to get through: one at 80 cm to 100 cm for a main bund, one between 35 and 40 for a secondary, and the spillways are meant to carry the excess. If you have more than one, or a main bund with a smaller secondary one, that is what the whole plan is for. Take them to ICAT, which is also where the main bund dimensions come from.

per_item.reference: Tell her the discard list first, because it is the easy part: leave out any egg that is too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Then the handling, which is where most people lose their chicks: collect the eggs every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them within seven to ten days at most. Set them pointed end down. Give a broody hen twelve to fourteen and no more. The incubation is twenty-one days and the hatching rate to expect is near 70 percent, so she should not be disappointed by a few that do not come out. Those figures are from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference for commercial local hens.

history.content: My sister keeps hens and asks which eggs she should save for hatching.

draws.answer: Tell her which two you keep, and explain why, not which way round. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to keep the ones that are colored like this, with a pointed end toward the face: it is the way to see the bird. It also says the brooder handles small hatchings in series, which is the same as keeping your own chicks with you rather than buying them, and the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks is the minimum, so if she is sizing her own flock from the reference's own figures, she is well above the minimum. Tell her what to do with the other ones: keep them seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, and sort out the ones that are too dirty, those that have no pointed end, or those that are too small, which are exactly those she should not set. And tell her to do the same work yourself if she can, since the reference says the brooder is meant to be used soon after hatching.

Tell her the four you have and why, because the method is to collect twelve to fourteen daily and keep them seven to ten days at most before setting. Tell her the natural way first: collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and sort them before setting, discarding the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Tell her to set pointed end down, one for about ten days at most, in a box with a soft material such as straw, and to keep her own name with her. And tell her the answer to what happens after the setting: discard any bird that has been eating too many worms, and if she still has it, take it to a livestock auxiliary.

per_item.reference: Collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry. Then sort them and throw out the ones that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked, or that have no pointed end. Keep them seven to ten days at most before setting them, and set them pointed end down. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs. Expect a hatching rate near seventy percent, which is the figure the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on.

history.content: How do I choose which eggs to put under the hen?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names them: small to medium in size, about 700 grams in all, laid once a day, under a cover, sheltered from wind and rain, with the hen resting, and kept seven to ten days at most. Tell her to set them pointed end down, in that order: three to six eggs, one to two days old, then a set of twenty-one. Give her a brooding hen as well as hers, and set them pointed end down as well. If she is busy with work, take her out of the way and put them when she is still.

Collect every day, kept somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them pointed end down. Count about ten to twelve per hen per laying and keep them seven to ten days at most. Keep them seven to ten days at most. I do not have a method for selecting them, so ask ICAT, which holds the reference, and I will not give you a way to choose them.

per_item.reference: Then bring the greenery to them, which is exactly what the 2017 ESFT compendium provides for: hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. Add the other free extras while you are at it, termites and maggots, which go on top of the formula whatever the age, with caterpillars for the youngest. On the housing itself, the arrangement asked for is a fenced run rather than a closed building, since a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one and lets you watch the birds better; a fenced and covered run may answer both your problem and that one. Keep the ground around clear, since a tuft of grass shelters the animals that bring disease.

history.content: My hens are shut in all day because of the hawks and I cannot let them out.

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is for keeping a henhouse well attended, not for shutting it in. Tell me where the birds spend most of their time and whether there are openings, and tell me the distance they would need to travel to reach the farm. Then tell me what you are selling, because hens that are not open are hens that do not give.

Then two things the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference has you with. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial village compendium says a henhouse of at least five compartments is what limits the spread, and it says the compartment wall should be roomy, well aired and roomy, and that tarpaulins are used to close against rain and wind. So the answer is to keep the opening in the building, not to close it. And call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see a bird that is sick, or that bites other birds, or that you do not recognise.

per_item.reference: Feed first, and enough of it to be ahead rather than catching up. Feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it is needed from day one: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day, and young birds from 61 days to sale about 5 kg in all at 25 to 35 grams a day. With it, buy the litter and the disinfectant, and arrange the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines with the animal health worker, since for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. Have the vitamins and dewormer to hand. And make sure the water is right before anything else: freely available, drinkers never empty, clean, in the shade and renewed at least twice a day.

history.content: What do I buy in the first week, before the birds start laying?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names four things you will need in the first weeks, before the flock starts laying. Feeders of the right size for the age: 50 cm long for a hen and 50 cm wide, 17 cm high, 22 for chicks, 17 cm high, 12 for the growers. Waterers of the same size as the feeders. The brooder for the chicks, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, 42 chicks. And the nest boxes, 0.5 cubic metres, 2 m by 2 m by 10 cm high, 26 chicks. For the laying start, the reference advises culling the poor layers and selling the cocks.

Feeders and waterers rather than breeder feed, which is the order the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives. For a flock of 60 hens and 6 cocks the first three months of keeping are spent buying the feed and selling the birds, so the first week is feeding rather than selling. Feeders of 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, three in the 2020 reference, 50 kg per hundred birds for chicks and 10 kg per hundred for a hen, and waterers of 50 cm by 50 by 5 for each bird, counted at 600 birds in all. Buy the cakes, millet beer draff, fish meal, bone salt and the vitamins from the suppliers, not at the counter.

per_item.reference: About two months in the main season. In Maritime and Plateaux the maize brochure puts the clearing in February and March, a little before the first rains, then the ploughing at those first rains in April and May, and the sowing in April to May once the rains are settled. So clearing runs ahead of sowing by roughly two months. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes the same sequence sits two months later, clearing in April and May and sowing in June and July.

history.content: How much time do I have between clearing and sowing in the Plateaux?

draws.answer: In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, the maize plot is prepared in July and cleared in August and September. Then the plot is ploughed at the first rains in April and May, then sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May. So clearing is at the first rains and sowing comes later once the rains are settled, not at the same time. The second season plot in Centrale, Kara and Savanes is chosen in January, cleared in February and March, and sown when the rains are settled in April to May.

The catalogue does not give a time gap at all, and I would rather say that plainly than invent one. What it says about the plot is that the ploughing comes at the first rains, around April to May for the main season, and the ploughing is done before the season starts, not after.
