The sowing comes when the rains are properly settled, around March to April for the main season, and the plot is prepared before that, clearing and ploughing going at the first rains. Ask ICAT for your prefecture.

per_item.reference: A group, if you can manage it. The catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, and it gives the reason plainly: one household rarely has the labour for it. The volumes show why, since 100 m of main bund is something like 17 to 25 cubic metres of earth. There is a second instruction about the site itself that is easy to overlook: replant elsewhere the trees you clear from it. So the work is a group undertaking and the clearing carries an obligation with it.

history.content: Who should be doing this lowland work?

draws.answer: The catalogue puts the work in the hands of a group: a farmers' organisation, and it says that for large areas of land such as a lowland developed from rainwater collection. So the work belongs to a group, not to one person. Among the people it names who can carry it is ICAT, because they are for the development of the hydrological sites, and ANAMET for the rain measurement, with its two poles, one of 80 cm by 30 by 12 for the main bund, and one of 70 by 40 by 6 for the secondary ones.

The catalogue does not say, and I am not going to fill you in on it. What it says is that the lowlands belong to you, and it puts the work to you: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, then move the earth along the plan, building the bunds to 80 to 100 cm at the lower base and 35 to 40 cm at the top, watered as you build so they compact. It does not say who does it, or when, and it does not say the labour itself. What I would not do is name the people, because the catalogue gives no contact. What I can tell you is not a question for a farming advice session: which organisation to approach for planning, or for the specific labour, is outside the text.

per_item.reference: I cannot say true or false, because the catalogue offers no measurement to judge it by. The practices themselves it sets out exactly: alley cropping, windbreaks, live hedges, assisted natural regeneration, Taungya, composting and simple lowland development. For measured effects, ask ICAT.

history.content: True or false: these practices are proven to offset climate change by a measurable amount.

draws.answer: False, as the catalogue states they are what the practice is for, not a solution to climate change. Its own example is that the trees are planted in areas where there was no tree before, so that the planting actually replaces what was lost. The rest of the catalogue presents these as ways of making the agricultural sector more resilient to the effects of climate change. For how much they actually offset, ICAT.

The catalogue does not say whether they offset climate change, so I have no answer to give you. What it does say is the same way to use them: write your own figures in the same rows, put them beside the practice names, and say what you measured rather than what someone else said. The six it gives are: lowland drainage and water control; water points; healthy soil; a rotation; the use of a Mucuna cover; composting animal droppings and plant debris; and tree planting, especially in the dry savanna zone. The catalogue stops there, with no cost and no measure of impact, no date and no supplier list. If you want to know how much carbon they hold, ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: False, at least on the time. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens in that reference, and it adds a warning worth hearing: at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. A brooding hen, by contrast, sits on twelve to fourteen eggs at a time.

history.content: True or false: an incubator hatches faster than a hen.

draws.answer: False. A gas incubator of 300 eggs takes about 210 days, and a flock of 60 hens takes about 1.3 kg of feed a day, not a few hours for a machine. The natural way, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, is to hatch for other keepers as well, so the eggs collect rather quickly. The incubation lasts twenty-one days.

False. The reference says both methods take 21 days for a cock and 30 days for a hen, and it says to watch the hatching rather than to hatch, because the eggs have to be kept cool and airy. The incubation itself takes twenty-one days either way, so the machine does not hatch faster. What the machine does do is be present during it: it sits in the room with you, takes the eggs, keeps them to cool, and throws the chicks out when they are ready.

per_item.reference: I do not have that figure and I will not guess at it, because a wrong temperature costs you the whole setting. history.content: What temperature should I set the incubator to?

I do not know that, and I will not guess it. What I can tell you about keeping the eggs, in any case: cool, airy and dry, the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for seven to ten days at most, somewhere safe.

per_item.reference: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the appearance, the weight, the ratio and the culling age. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Appearance: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb. Live weight at six months: about 1.5 kg for a cock, against about 1.3 kg for a hen. Ratio: one cock for ten hens, which is what gives the minimum nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Culling: at 24 months, for cocks and hens alike, where the 2017 ESFT compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. The reason it gives for all that care is one sentence: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.

history.content: What does the reference specify for the breeding cock?

draws.answer: Two things. He should be vigorous and agile, a cock with a well developed bright red comb. And he should be well fed, vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, because the cock determines the health of the chicks. Those are the two things to look at when you buy him, and it is worth buying two cocks, because a cock that is too small is one of the ways breeding does not come up well. After the chick hatches, you should keep the cock with the hens at a ratio of one cock for ten hens.

Six points, in 2020 terms. At six months a cock weighs about 1.5 kg, with a real tail between them, and he should be vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb. The reason it gives is that the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and it sets the ratio: one cock for ten hens. Selling breeding cocks is named as one of the two ways of keeping back breeding birds, alongside selling the chicks. It also warns against visiting other farms, because the cock decides whether the birds you bring are healthy.

per_item.reference: Where: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, which has two rainy seasons; FAO GIEWS puts the second around October. Not in Kara or Savanes, which have one; Centrale can behave either way. Plot chosen: July, against January for the main season. Character: the shorter of the two seasons. Risk: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so the crop needs an improved tolerant variety. Corresponding note for the north: late sowings are where the same virus does its damage there, so late sowing should be avoided. Referrals: ICAT for the prefecture's calendar, ANAMET for this year's rains.

history.content: Set out the second season.

draws.answer: Year one, the improved varieties released there: TZEE W Pop STR QPM for 75 to 85 days, QPM for 90 to 95, Amen for white grain, AB11 for 90 to 100 days, Ikenne 9449 SR for 90 to 100, Obatanpa for 100 to 110 days. In the south: Maritime and Plateaux, plot chosen January, cleared February and March, ploughed at the first rains April and May, sown when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, so January to April. In the north, Kara and Savanes, plot chosen April, cleared April and May, ploughed and sown April to May. Centrale sits between the two and follows the southern example. The rule that applies everywhere: sow when it rains regularly, never on one isolated shower.

per_item.reference: It matters, and the reason is written in the 2017 ESFT compendium: the choice of the cock is capital if you want chicks of good size and in good health. At six months a local cock weighs about 1.5 kg against about 1.3 kg for a hen. Keep one cock for about ten hens, and change the breeding cocks when they stop performing.

history.content: Does the choice of the cock really matter, or can I take any cock? Justify your answer.

Choose the vigorous, agile, agile, strong birds, cockerels or local hens, and keep them near the cock. Then you are bound to beat the others: cocks that do not take well to a cock and to a hen are taken out. What matters most about the cock from my own study is that he is vigorous and agile. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives two reasons why a cock is required for a breeding nucleus, and they are worth stating before you buy one: it gives a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, and it states that a cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. per_item.reference: There is no single date, and giving you one would cost you the crop. The window depends on where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And inside that window the signal is the rain, not the date, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Sow when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. ANAMET can tell you what this season is doing.

history.content: Just give me one date to sow, I do not want regions and seasons.

draws.answer: Sow at the first rains, not on one specific date, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. The two regions, Maritime and Plateaux, have two rainy seasons. Centrale sits between and can behave either way. For your prefecture, ANAMET gives this season's onset and forecasts; for a real date, ask the local radio. The country's general calendar is five rains roughly May to September, with January for sowing.

I cannot give you one date, because the guidance I have is regional and seasonal. For exactly one date, ask ICAT, which holds the calendar of your prefecture. The useful rains do not start on the same date every year, and knowing the prefecture is the right step but the timing is not. What I can tell you to do while you wait is prepare the plot in advance so you are ready to sow the moment the rains are truly established, and to plant only when they are reliably rain.

per_item.reference: Take two or three names rather than one, with their cycles, so you are not stuck if the first is out of stock. Know which constraint applies to your field: striga points to TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, short rains to Amen. Know the cycle your season carries, from the range on the list, 75 to 85 days at the short end up to 105 to 115. And know the averages rather than the potentials, since the potential is the yield when growing conditions are good. Go to an approved seller, since the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else, and ask ICAT or ITRA which suits your region this season.

history.content: What should I take with me to the seed seller?

draws.answer: Take the cycle, the potential and the average yields together with the list of specific problems for your variety, because that is what the sowing information is for. Tell him the length of your season and the rains you usually get. And tell him what the seed carries, because the brochure's wording is that choosing the variety is one of the decisions you make now and it costs him a seed.

Take the five the ITRA and ICAT brochure lists with you. The seed is obtained from an approved seller, and that is worth telling you about: buying improved seed from them is what the brochure's own instruction is for. So come with your own small grain or legume pile, not with a bag of seed. And bring the variety itself, since it says the cycle and the yield must fit your region and your rains.

per_item.reference: That may be the projection working rather than the farm failing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, which is very little, and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two. It explains the difference by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges, so what you are living through is the thin part. Two things to check rather than despair. Are you selling all three products, birds, eggs and droppings, since the projection counts all three? And do you have buyers arranged before each batch, with a client register and contracts where you can get them? If both are yes, hold on through the second year. Take your own figures to ICAT and compare them against the study line by line.

history.content: I have been running a year now and I have barely made anything.

draws.answer: The study does not say, and I would rather say so than speculate. Its figures are 391,000 FCFA of first year working capital against 2,790,400 FCFA of first year selling, in 2020 prices, and its net result is only 89,000 FCFA in year one against 3,700,000 in year two. Those are 2020 evaluations for one unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, so they apply to one farm and not to what you are building. Use them as your own year to build it, not as a template. ICAT holds the study and can help you see whether it fits your own figures.

That is the test the method is for, and it is easy to miss. The annual averages come from the five years the catalogue records in a band: 7 to 10 tonnes a hectare of potential, 2 to 3 of actual, and all of it is against one maize. So take your own yields to ICAT, which is the office for this measurement in your region, and read through the averages before you spend anything else. If your average is near 4 tonnes, then the profit is not near zero, and if it is near 8, then the profit is near 10, not a whole cent.

per_item.reference: Feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Clean water matters most of all, because chicks die easily of dehydration; never let the drinker be empty. From 1 to 60 days a bird eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day. Keep the mother hen with them for the first weeks: she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries.

draws.answer: Four things, counted per hundred grams. Energy: 57.5, from maize, sorghum, millet or fonio; legumes, 15 to 30, soya, cowpea, tchouck. Protein, 10 to 25, from groundnut, cowpea, fish, blood meal, soya or cowpea protein, and cottonseed or palm-kernel cake. Minerals, 5 to 15, then salt. Fruits and vegetables, 10 to 25, whatever the age. Water, freely available at all times, in the shade, clean. Give the chick feeders their own feed, from age one, so they do not compete with the adults.

Feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. On top, give them clean water constantly, and a drinker that they can reach is useful in the run. Clean it often and wash it with you rather than let it sit.

per_item.reference: The arrangement the catalogue actually shows is alternating, a line of maize and a line of soya. It does not describe mixing within the line, so I will not recommend something it does not offer. What it does give you for judging any arrangement is the six points to respect: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs and the period over which the two crops share the plot. And the spacings, pure, are maize 80 cm by 40 cm and soya 40 cm by 20 cm, with the instruction to widen the maize pockets when associating. ICAT for your plot.

history.content: Alternate lines, or mix the two crops in the same line?

draws.answer: The brochure gives them as one practice, and says how to carry it out rather than which way to take. The maize then soya in the same plot, the two grown in rotation instead of one grown alone, and maize then cowpea, groundnut or cassava in rotation. It gives the maize then cowpea as the example of a rotation well tolerated there, and the sowing distances between varieties too. Ask ICAT which of the two suits your plot.

The brochure answers both: alternating, with maize at the head, then a legume such as cowpea or soybean, then back to maize. Mixing is what the catalogue calls a succession of crops in time on the same plot, and it gives an example of it in the south, maize then cowpea then maize then cowpea, or maize then cassava then cowpea then maize. The rule it puts before that is that the root system of the plants used should not compete for resources.

per_item.reference: In the shade, and the catalogue leaves no room on this one. Its first step says the site must be a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, meaning the wind and the rain, and it adds that a water point is an advantage. So all three conditions point the same way: you keep the heap out of the sun, out of the wind and out of the rain, and you bring the water to it yourself, layer by layer, as you build. The catalogue does not say what goes wrong in the open, so I will not tell you what would happen. I will only tell you that its instruction is shade.

history.content: Should I put the heap in the open where the sun can work on it, or in the shade?

draws.answer: The catalogue says the site is the place to put the build, but it gives no instruction on shade. It gives these four things about the building: a heap of residues, wood ash, topsoil, or well rotted compost as the activator; a little manure on the site; and water laid on the site after the building is raised. It gives no weather condition to worry about, so I am not going to put a shade plan on me. What I can tell you that is useful in any case is the size, at least 1.5 m by 2 m, one compartment of 0.6 m by 1 m, three bricks at most, and the watering after the heap is laid. For shade, ask ICAT.

In the shade, and the catalogue says that in order for the decomposing material to decompose well, you must keep the heap in a shaded place. The opening is the one part where the shade matters: the catalogue says to open a shallow drainage channel and not to keep the heap closed. So the answer is to open the heap and not to close it, and then keep the shade. The rest is what the heap does for the heap itself: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator.

per_item.reference: Then do the cleaning now and the disinfection when you have the rest, because goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask are all compulsory and the reference gives that as an instruction not to skip. The cleaning is worth doing on its own: a good cleaning of the building already removes a good part of the germs. Sweep the inside, and keep to two or three times a week from now on, throwing the droppings into the manure pit well away from the building. Wash the feeders and drinkers, and keep washing them every day. Clear the ground outside, because a tuft of grass shelters snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. Then get the goggles and mask, and plan the disinfection for when the compartment is empty between batches, using caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent or quicklime at 10 percent, after changing the litter.

history.content: I want to clean out the henhouse properly for the first time.

Good. Tell me whether the birds are in it at the moment, and whether you have goggles, gloves and a gas mask, because those two answers change what you can do this week. The order of work is fixed: separation, then cleaning, then disinfection.
The birds are in there and I have gloves but nothing else.

draws.answer: Then two of the four are missing and the gas mask will not cover them. Separation is the first of the four, which the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to do straight away for any bird showing signs of disease. Clean it first: sweep the inside of the henhouse, because a tuft of unwashed hair holds a good part of the swill, and throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from it. Then the disinfection, which you do after the cleaning, with caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent or quicklime at 10 percent, wearing goggles, gloves and a gas mask. Check the wall heights against the 1.2 m high wall you want before you open it: the 2017 ESFT compendium recommends openings of 0.5 to 1 m for a henhouse opening onto a run, so that the animals do not wander. Then look at the feeders and drinkers, which you replace and clean regularly, and look for a solution for disease in the droppings as well, since they are one of the ways disease moves: the same references say to disinfect the litter and to take out the dead animals fast and buried or burnt.

Then two things without a mask, and I would rather say them plainly. Wear goggles, because you see. Wear gloves, because you handle the droppings and the swill. And have a plan for what you are doing, which is the cheapest part of all: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts the five stages of cleaning a henhouse, separation, cleaning, disinfection, disinfection with a disinfectant, and rebuilding the litter, in order. Do not wait for an outbreak, do not wait for a bird to fall ill. Keep the feeders full, the drinkers full and washed, and the manure pit well away from the building. And look at the birds: the 2017 ESFT compendium says that a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, because it allows you to watch the birds. If this is the first time and you can do nothing about it, that is a real question for the veterinary service of your village, because neither one nor the veterinary service can tell you whether it is worth it.

per_item.reference: I have no way to know that. I work offline and I do not see today's markets, and a number I made up would cost you money. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does carry an egg figure, 100 FCFA, but it is a 2020 evaluation used to build a projection of 2,376 eggs sold in the first year, not a price for this week and not a price for Lome in particular. ICAT can help you turn whatever price you find into a calculation you can use.

history.content: What is a tray of eggs worth in Lome right now?

draws.answer: I cannot give you a price for eggs. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference prices eggs by volume and does not quote a price for a tray, and a price in Lomé would have been a figure I would have. What I can tell you is what is available: about 1.5 kg of eggs, 28 days, set pointed end down, kept seven to ten days at most in a cool airy place, that is what the 2017 ESFT village compendium counts. For a current price, ask a local or listen to the radio.

I cannot tell you, and I will not guess. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference prices a hen in lay at 1005 FCFA, and a bird in lay at 57,000 FCFA, and those are evaluations from one point in time, not a price to find. What changes is the market, which is what a buyer request makes. per_item.reference: In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops, and the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists the common combinations: maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices adds maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. If you associate, widen the spacing between the pockets.

history.content: What crops can I grow together with my maize?

draws.answer: The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists two groups and puts maize in neither. The improving varieties that run pure trees: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM, pool5, Amen, Obatanpa. The varieties that go well with them. Alongside the maize it also puts cowpea, groundnut and cassava among the crops that can share the plot with it, in the same band. For which variety suits your region this season, ask ICAT.

The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists the associations it counts most often: maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. It gives no reason for those associations, and it does not say which of the 10 varieties goes with which. Ask ICAT for what suits your region this season, and ask the extension adviser who knows the region.

per_item.reference: The brochure does not deal with part of a plot, so I will not invent a rule for it. What it says applies to a field with striga in it: use a striga tolerant maize variety, together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. The pulling is clearly local and you would do it where the striga is. The variety choice is not, since you sow one field. And a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, so it applies to the plot as a whole. ICAT can look at the actual spread.

history.content: Only part of the plot has striga. Do I treat the whole thing?

draws.answer: Treating for striga is the same way as treating for nitrogen loss: use a striga tolerant maize variety together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. Use an amination such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in rotation and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. Do not cut the striga stems into anything. And if you need help choosing the tolerant variety or deciding on a rotation, ICAT.

The brochure asks for a combination, and it gives two reasons why you should not treat part of it. The striga germines live in the soil, and a uniform striga-free plot means the weed is less frequent. And it says that if striga appears in a corner, the whole plot can become striga, so a spot treatment is not worth the land. If you have a small piece where striga is present, take it to ICAT for the variety that is tolerant to striga, and to take the rotation that suits your plot.

per_item.reference: Then two separate things to do. For the chicks themselves, put the few with dull down where you can watch feeding and health closely rather than losing them in the crowd; that is one of the four reasons the brooder exists, and it holds 60 chicks in 0.6 cubic metres for their first three weeks. Give all of them clean water in their own drinker, never empty, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, because chicks die easily of dehydration, and feed them apart from any adults so they do not have to compete. For the farm, the new chicks are new stock arriving: the rule is two weeks of quarantine for any bird that comes in, bought or given, so keep them clear of your thirty hens for that time. Watch both groups for the signs of a sick bird while they are apart, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see them.

history.content: How do I know if the chicks I bought are any good?

Look at each bird against four points: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Tell me what you are seeing and I can say whether it is something to act on. It would also help to know whether you already keep birds, because chicks arriving onto a farm with a flock raise a separate question.
Most of them look right, a few have dull down, and yes I have about thirty hens already.

draws.answer: Then two things to do. Collect the eggs every day, keep them seven to ten days at most somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them pointed end down. If any of the chicks was sad, too thin, drowsy and drowsy with a dull coat, or had no bright colouring, put it down too soon, in the brooder rather than out in the open. If most of your chicks look right, and the few with the dull down, you should watch the feed and the water closely: chicks die easily of dehydration, and chicks that are too small are not growing into healthy birds. Keep the mother hen with them for the first weeks, because she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. And look for the signs in the feed as well as the chicks: a healthy newly hatched chick hatches after twelve to fourteen grams in the first days, against about three to four for the youngest. Take the eggs to a registered breeder or to ICAT, or to a livestock auxiliary if you cannot watch them.

Then two things are worth checking. Look for the signs of a well developed body and a well formed combs and wattles, which the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for in the description of a good hatch. And check the feed; chicks need about 1.5 kg of feed a day, roughly 1.5 kg per 100 kg of feed, and they must never be left without water, which is what the brooder is for. Buy from a well followed farm or an ITRA/ICAT registered supplier, and keep the feeders for the adults too, so they do not have to compete. If any of your chicks look weak, or if you keep more than three or four, take them to ICAT, who will see it.

per_item.reference: Main bund: width at the lower base 80 to 100 cm; width at the top 35 to 40 cm; height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: width at the lower base 70 to 80 cm; width at the top 25 to 30 cm; height 25 to 30 cm. Construction: watered as they are built so that they compact.
