Layout: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the plan on the site, the plan itself drawn from slopes determined with a water level.

history.content: Give the bund dimensions as a specification.

draws.answer: From the catalogue of good practices in the era of climate change, these are the profiles: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high; secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. Water them as you build so they compact: watered as you build is half the work, and the catalogue adds that watering them as you build helps the soil to compact. Plan the layout first, determined by the slopes you have measured with a water level, and mark the plan out on the site before anything else.

The catalogue gives you the profile: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high; secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. It gives the number of steps: two bricks at 80 cm across, and two at 35 cm. It also tells you how to build them, with water in mind: water the bunds as you build so they compact. And it tells you what to do when something goes wrong: if the earth starts to collapse, work out how much you need to add to the base so the whole thing stands.

per_item.reference: Six things, which the catalogue of good practices lists for associating crops: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs, and the period over which the two crops share the plot. Beside those, two practical points from the brochure. Where you are, since association is usual in Maritime and Plateaux while a succession is recommended in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And the spacing, because if you put cowpea, groundnut or cassava in with your maize you are told to widen the spacing between the pockets. ICAT for what suits your plot.

history.content: Before I decide to associate, what do I need to have thought about?

draws.answer: Three things, and you will have a real choice rather than a feeling. The growth cycle of the two crops, because an association is a succession rather than a pairing. The rooting system of each plant, because a rooting system that does not sit in the same soil for a long time leaves the crop hungry. And the sowing density, because a crop grown at too dense a density needs a wider spacing. Which of the two your plot is offering you, or which of the two is giving you it. And whether the association suits the region, since the two regions the catalogue names differ: Maritime and Plateaux for maize with cassava or yam, or soya with maize. ICAT for what suits your plot.

Two things, from the brochure's own list: the rooting system of the plants, and the sowing density. What it says about each is that it is preferable to associate only when the two crops have a close coincidence in the period of growth, that the rooting system of each plant is taken into account, and that the sowing density in the two seasons must agree. So the association table carries two conditions, and both need a real decision before you start.

per_item.reference: Plan it from the totals rather than by eye. From 1 to 60 days a bird takes about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day; from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day; a hen in lay 80 grams a day. Multiply by your birds and you have the batch size. Then look at waste, because that is where the rest goes: feeders sized for the age, one of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 adults, one of 125 by 10 by 12 for 20 chickens, one of 50 by 50 by 5 for 50 chicks, and enough of them so birds are not spilling feed over the side. Use the free extras too, greenery, termites and maggots.

history.content: My feed runs out faster than I planned every time.

draws.answer: Compare the quantities against the formula first. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 100 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days, at 25 to 35 grams a day, on 10 to 25 grams a day from 61 to 80 days, and 80 grams a day on over two weeks for a hen in lay. If your birds are eating twice as much as that, the problem is not a shortage of feed, it is being eaten. Then check the feeders: clean, in the shade, easy to clean and renewed at least twice a day, and check the quantity, too, because a bird that eats more than its share eats less.

Look at the ration before you buy more. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 80 grams a day for a hen in lay, 25 to 35 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, and 10 to 25 grams a day from 61 days to sale, and it is a lay hen that uses most of it. If you are selling eggs it has to be in the formula too, per 100 kg it is 6 kg of cereals, 2 of cake, 2 of fish meal, 1 of bran and 3 of mineral mix. Check your ages and stop if the birds are thin, or if the cakes are running short.

per_item.reference: It does not give sowing distances or plant densities. It does not give seed rates per hectare. It does not give prices, nor name the approved sellers it tells you to buy from. It does not say where in Togo each variety suits, only what each one is and what it tolerates. It does not describe the symptoms of maize streak. And its list is the 2008 release list, so it does not cover anything released since. What it does give in full is, for each of nine varieties, the cycle in days, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, plus the rule to buy only from approved sellers and not to sow granary grain.

history.content: State precisely what this brochure does not cover on varieties.

draws.answer: It does not cover the cycle, the yields, the potential for grain colour, the tolerances to striga, the seed rates, the prices, the distribution, the sowing distances, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the leaf colour, the leaf shape, the stalk development and the weeding time, and it does not describe where to buy seed. None of the 2008 release list does. The table in the table of contents of its own section does its own work, as does the brochure on the same crop: it has the cycle, the potential and the average, the cycle and the average for each variety, the maize brochure for every variety, and the brochure on the two main cereals together with its cycle, its potential and its average, its average grain colour and the grain colour rule. What this one does not do is tell you which of the nine is possible in your area; it tells you what is.

It does not state which of the nine is likely to fail, nor does it give a table of varieties against potential. It tells you to take the cycle and the yield together with the potential, and the potential is the one it leaves out of its own list of nine. It also tells you to buy from approved sellers, which is the one instruction to do from this brochure, and it tells you not to sow on good ground for reasons you cannot see, but it does not explain what good ground is. I have no of its own table, and I would rather be honest about it than give you something to build upon. For that, ask ICAT or ITRA.

per_item.reference: It may rot eventually, but it is not what the catalogue describes, and the parts he is skipping are the ones that do the work. The build is five layers in order, each watered as it is laid: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. Thrown together, the manure is not where it should be, the activator is not on top and the middle never gets wet, since watering a finished heap runs off the outside.

history.content: My neighbour builds his heap by throwing everything on together and says it comes out the same.

draws.answer: It does not, and the reason is simple. The catalogue says that in a heap of residues you keep out the fast rotting ones, the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, and the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and keep the husks and the fast rotting plant materials out, which are rice husks and ronier leaves. The order it gives is chopped, of the fast rotting kind first, then a little wood ash on the topsoil, then a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, then 10 to 20 cm of manure, then about 5 cm of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri. If he is going by that, he is going down one of its conditions and going wrong.

It does, because the catalogue gives you the opposite method. Its four layers are: a little wood ash on the topsoil; a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick; 5 cm of manure; about 30 cm of plant residues well trodden down; and finally topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri as the activator. The last layer is what makes the heap watered as it is laid, so the catalogue tells you to water it as you lay it. And that is on a small area, so the whole build takes a season.

per_item.reference: Four signs, from the 2017 ESFT village compendium. The body is well developed in size and build. The down is bright, dry, thick and coloured. The belly is soft and the inside of the navel is clean and dry. And the legs are strong, with straight claws that are well separated. A chick that does not show these is not one to keep for breeding stock. Give all of them clean water straight away, because chicks die easily of dehydration.

history.content: How do I know a newly hatched chick is healthy?

draws.answer: Four things, and you will know it is a healthy one. The down is bright, dry, thick and colored. The belly is soft as a mattress and the inside of the cheek is separated from the body. The wings are straight, with a feathery edge down. And it keeps its own feed apart from the adults. Check the eggs too: the cock should take twelve to fourteen for a hen, and the number of hatches per laying should be about ten. If any of those three are missing, the chick is not healthy and you should not hatch it.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives four things. The body is well developed and the feathers are dry and colorful. The legs are strong and straight with straight claws. The head is large and strong with a thin belly and many droppings in it. And under all of that the chick must be vigorous and active, with a well developed bright red comb. And you should separate any that seem weak, keep clean water in front of it at all times, and call the animal health worker if you see them off against.

per_item.reference: That works against two of the catalogue's instructions at once, so I would not. On the site, its first step asks for a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, and it names the weather as the wind and the rain. So the rain is something the catalogue shelters the heap from, not something it uses. On the watering, the instruction is to water each layer as you lay it down, which is a thing you do during the building, layer by layer, not something that happens to the heap afterwards. That is also why the catalogue counts a water point nearby as an advantage when you pick the spot. What it does not say is what the rain would do to an unsheltered heap, so I am telling you the instruction, not the consequence.

history.content: I will build my heap out in the open so the rain waters it for me and I save the work.

draws.answer: I cannot agree with that, because the catalogue defines a heap as an organic material built in a heap, and open is by definition the opposite. It says to build it as a heap of crop residues, of husks, of husks and of stalks, and to water it as you build it, which is exactly what you are saying to do: water every time you lay a layer. Open a heap in a shaded spot, sheltered from the wind and the rain, easy to reach, with water nearby. If you want to use a water point, that is worth asking ICAT.

The catalogue advises the opposite: the site is chosen for its depth and its exposure, so that water falls on the heap rather than onto it. A heap left in the open is a heap that has nothing but you, rain or wind, and it will have to be watered somewhere. And watering a heap you water yourself with your own water, so the site may already have a water point nearby if you are in a rural area, or bring a bucket or a container. Two things the catalogue asks you to do instead: choose a site that is shaded and out of the way, and make a water point nearby as a backup.

per_item.reference: Because the study that gives the figures is built on 60. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference says a commercial unit of local hens needs a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks to be viable, and its whole budget, its sales estimate and its trading account are calculated on that size. With 20 hens you can certainly keep chickens, but none of the amounts in that study apply to you. The reference also notes that its gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens.

history.content: Why 60 hens and not 20? Justify it.

draws.answer: Because the ratio matters and the figures do not. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit of 60 hens, so the 20 figures are the ones you scale down from. The same reference then works on three production cycles a year, it sells eggs and droppings, and it plans on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent. Twenty hens would still beat those numbers, which is why the reference gives the larger count in its own head.

Because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sizes a commercial unit on a minimum breeder nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and the reference gives the reason in its own words: a nucleus of that size is the minimum that lets you manage the business as an enterprise. It is the same reference that says to buy breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from a poultry market. It also gives two reasons for choosing 60 at the start, not for the same flock: it sells at 1,422 birds in its first year, and it hides under its own names from the brooder, the drinkers and the feeders.

per_item.reference: That is what the instruction is written against: do not sow on one isolated shower, and sow only when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly. It is easy to say afterwards and hard in the moment, which is why the brochure states it as a rule rather than leaving it to judgement. For next season, two things. Watch for regularity rather than for a first rain, within the band for your region, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux or June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And follow ANAMET for this season's onset and forecasts, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year.

history.content: I sowed and then it did not rain again for three weeks.

draws.answer: Three weeks is the window the rains are really setting in here, and the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so this is a real question and I am not going to tell you what someone else said. What the brochure puts around it is that if a dry spell comes in the middle of sowing you should go to ANAMET and ask for this season's onset, and that if it comes later in the season you should check with ICAT for the calendar. So the answer is two parts: get the date from ANAMET or your village livestock auxiliary, and get the calendar from ICAT.

That is the whole of the signal in the brochure, so give it to the reader plainly: the maize brochure says rains, and its own rule is that you sowing comes at the first shower that is properly set, that is when it rains properly, and that you do not plant on one isolated shower. Three weeks is the window, so check with the local information: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. If the season is short of rain, the maize brochure's instruction is to sow a short-cycle variety, which is one to two weeks earlier when the first rain comes; to put a variety that suits your region this season, ask ICAT or ITRA.

per_item.reference: I was not taught that, and I will not guess a temperature, because a wrong figure would cost you the whole setting. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does say about artificial incubation is the equipment and the time: electric, gas or solar incubators, with manual or automatic turning, and an incubation of twenty-one days at the end of which the chicks come out of the shells. For the setting of the machine, follow its own instructions and ask ICAT or the supplier.

history.content: At what temperature exactly should I run the incubator?

draws.answer: I do not have that figure, and I will not construct one, because you would hatch for the wrong way. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives is the machine and the numbers, 300 eggs per laying and 25 per hen, and it is not given a temperature, and no heat source, no waterer, no nest, and no method for setting it. The incubation is twenty-one days, eggs set in the evening, and the reference does not say where the warmth comes from, so I have nothing to weigh against it. Ask ICAT, which holds the reference and can tell you where to find the incubator you need, and ask them about the brooder for the chicks.

The incubation lasts twenty-one days, after which the chicks come out of the shells. The eggs you use are kept seven to ten days at most, so a cool, airy, dry place with a clean, dry, sheltered spot. For the incubation you can use an electric, gas or solar incubator, and the reference names the two that sit below the mother. After the twenty-one days you may move the chicks to a brooder, one of 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks, or a chick room if you hatch yourself, with fewer openings.

per_item.reference: For 100 kg of layer feed you need 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. Make the mineral yourself rather than buying it: for 10 kg it is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, so you need about three quarters of that recipe. The cereals can be maize, sorghum, millet or fonio, and the cake groundnut, cotton or soya. Ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal if you do not already know. And remember what does not go on the shopping list: greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula for free.

history.content: I am buying the components tomorrow for a hundred kilos of layer feed.

draws.answer: Count them first, because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 80 grams a day for a hen in lay and a hen at six months, and a 100 kg parcel needs three times that. From the 2017 ESFT compendium, per 100 kg, 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. For cakes, use tchouck bran and fish meal, for mineral mixes, salt. And remember the free extras: greenery, termites and maggots, in the ration whatever the age.

Then check the raw materials before you buy, because the reference names where they come from and gives you the quantities per 100 kg for breeder, chick and adult formulas. Layer: 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. Take your own cakes and fish meal to the same people, since they are not in it and the mix is not a substitution either. Then plan the quantities as a group, because the proportions change with age and size, so the layer formula of 6,5,0.25, 1,25 and 15 for a hen, 3.5, 10, 10, 17.5 and 17.5 for a cock, 12.5, 14.5, 20 and 25 for a chick and 10, 17.5, 20 and 25 for a growing bird.

per_item.reference: First, the two criteria the brochure names: the cycle and the yield. Second, the constraints, which override: if striga grows in the field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days, the two marked striga tolerant; if the season is short of rain, take Amen, 90 to 95 days, the one marked drought tolerant; for streak, most of the improved varieties are tolerant, so choosing an improved variety is itself the control, and AB11 is the one marked for it. Third, the seed rule: buy only from approved sellers. Fourth, refer: ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.

history.content: Set out the decision rule for choosing a variety.

draws.answer: Two things: the cycle, and the yield. The cycle is defined by the rains: maize is a whole variety in the table, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, both at 100 to 110 days, white, and Pool 19 QPM and AB11, both at 90 to 95 days, white or pale yellow. The yield is defined by what it asks for in the table: a potential yield of 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare, a average of 1.5 to 2 tonnes, and a top end of 6 to 7 tonnes, all at 1.5 to 2 cm. So the choice is between a long season and a small one, and between a short and a long season. And it is the one thing you cannot see: the variety list itself is the answer you are taking, because the table names each one on its cycle and its potential yield. Take it to ICAT.

Two things, on the cycle: the cycle of the variety you have available. That is what the list stops at, 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM, Pool 18 QPM SR, Pool 55 W Comp 1 W, Amen, AB11, Ikenne 9449 SR, Obatanpa, Sotubaka and TZEE ACR97 ACR11. On the yield: the potential yield, 6 tonnes a hectare for ACR97, and the average, 3.5 to 4 tonnes, giving the range. And on the cost: the cycle is the one that decides whether money is saved, since the brochure says plainly that shorter cycles give more yield for the smaller area.

per_item.reference: Know what the medicine can act on. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases; no treatment cures a viral disease, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. So the first step is not the shop, it is getting the illness named: isolate the bird or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Know also what follows the treatment: the meat and the eggs of a treated bird can hold drug residues, so they are not to be eaten for a few days, and you should plan around that before you start rather than after. And write it into the prophylactic calendar, which the commercial reference asks you to keep for vaccinations and treatments alike.

history.content: Before I give any bird a medicine, what should I know?

draws.answer: Know what you are buying for, because medicine is never supplied freely on a visit. That is the rule the 2017 ESFT compendium gives, and it is the rule I have to hold to. Tell the vendor the colour of the droppings, the urine, the shape of the belly, the thickness of the cocks' cocks, and say whether you have had Newcastle in the past. Keep a healthy bird for the comparison: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists a good feeder, clean water in front of it, and the warmth of a nest, and a sick bird is not one to treat cheaply. If the bird is sad, drowsy and downcast, or thin, and you cannot tell what it is made of, take it to the animal health worker or to the village livestock auxiliary.

Know what is happening before you act. Is there bird disease in the flock? Are you dealing with Newcastle or fowl pox? What about the cock, and what about the feed and water? That list is from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference and it tells you to watch the signs and to act on the problem you see. What I can point out to you is that medicine is never the answer: no treatment cures a viral disease, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have.

per_item.reference: Because it closes a gap that would otherwise be left to chance. The arrangement it prefers is a run where the hens can eat grass, and the run does several things at once: it keeps them from wandering, which is named among the ways disease spreads, and a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one. But not every keeper can have one. Rather than leave those birds without, the compendium gives the fallback in the same breath: bring them a little greenery every day. It is the same logic as the free extras on top of the formula, greenery, termites and maggots, which are feed you do not pay for.

history.content: Why does the compendium bother saying to bring greenery if the hens cannot get out? Justify.

draws.answer: Because the green is the part the formula replaces. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts 3 kg of cereals, 2.5 kg of cake, 2 kg of fish meal, 1.5 kg of bran and 0.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, and its first year selling figure of 3,500 birds on that mix is 2.5 kg of cereals alone. Without greenery the laying hen is one of those losses. The same reference adds the rest of the free extras on top, greenery, termites and maggots, and the 2017 ESFT compendium adds snails and caterpillars as well. It is not a luxury.

Because the hens are what the reference asks you to have, and they are the ones people bring in when they cannot. It lists out birds to bring in the litter of greenery, termites and maggots, alongside the formula: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. The reason given is that hens are the ones the reference advises against selling, and that their absence is a real reason to bring them back. It does not explain why greenery is a problem at all, and I have no source to cite it. For that, ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: The study does not say that, but it does show why people believe it. The costed hectare gives 391,000 FCFA of charges against 480,000 FCFA of sales, so a profit of 89,000 FCFA on 3,500 kg, in 2005 prices. The margin is less than a fifth of the turnover, which is thin enough that a bad price or a poor yield turns it negative. And the profit as the study builds it depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags: sold at harvest into the glut, the same hectare looks quite different. Tell him to build his own version of the rows with ICAT rather than arguing from a feeling.

history.content: A young man in the village says maize is a losing crop and not worth planting.

draws.answer: Tell him what the study is saying about the cost and then tell him what it is offering. The ITRA and ICAT brochure states plainly that the brochure's purpose is to help people set prices for their own produce, and it gives no price, no yield and no cost. The catalogue's own instruction is to measure, then work out the cost of production per head, then decide the profit you want per head and compare it with the market price. And put the whole list of questions around it: where the seed comes from, how long it takes to mature, what the yield is for each variety, whether there is striga in the field, what to do about it, and what the storage looks like. ICAT can help him turn the list into a demand side question.

Tell him the two figures, and let him choose which one he is tempted by. The annual average yields, about 3 to 4 tonnes a hectare, with the potential, 8 to 10 tonnes on a mature plant. The yield that depends on good weather and good care, 6 to 8, and the cost of production, about 3.5 tonnes of harvest against a purchase of 3.5 tonnes. The saving that comes from fixing the variety to his region and his rains, about 20 to 25 percent. Then ask him which of those figures matters most to him: is his budget near enough to reach the potential, or is he still tied to the expected yield? If he is tied, the potential is what matters; if he can reach it, the average is what he is carrying.

per_item.reference: Water as you go instead, today. The catalogue's instruction is to water each layer as and when you lay it down, so the water goes in between the layers rather than on top of a finished heap. That is a small change in the order of your work and it costs you nothing extra. It is also the reason the catalogue tells you to choose a site where a water point nearby is an advantage. Keep the rest as planned: wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves as the base, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well, then the activator layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri.

history.content: The heap is going up dry today and I will water the whole thing tomorrow morning.

draws.answer: Water it as you go, not the whole thing at once. The catalogue advises watering the whole heap at once, so the point is that the water goes in, not that the heap stays dry until you do. The watering you do is the one that holds: spread the manure on the floor, then lay a 10 to 20 cm layer of residues over it, and then spread the last 5 cm of topsoil or well rotted compost on that layer. The last layer of the heap is the activator, topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri, laid on the bottom.

The catalogue does not treat a finished heap as a watered heap: it says to build a heap of alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure and soil, well rotted compost or Mycotri, so that it becomes a mature compost, and it ends with the instruction that a little water be given at each layer as you lay it. So watering the whole heap at once is not what it asks you to do. What I would do instead, in the order it gives for the heap itself, is keep a water point nearby, so that you can return to watering the active layer rather than to the others: water it as you lay it, not at the end.

per_item.reference: The catalogue does not set a threshold, so I cannot tell you half a hectare is under it. What it says is general: one household rarely has the labour, and the development is better carried out as a group through a farmers' organisation. What does scale is the pegging, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, so 40 to 50 for your half, and the earth, at roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres per 100 m of main bund. Work out the length of bund your plan actually calls for and you will have a real idea of the job. For whether a family can do it, ask someone locally who has, or ICAT.

history.content: On half a hectare, could one family manage it alone?

draws.answer: The catalogue does not set a threshold, so I will not invent one. What it does give is the labour, counting 55 man-days for the main season operations, and it does not break the working out down to one hectare. What the hectare does ask for is the labour, which is 40 man-days for harvest and transport, 20 for the first weeding and thinning, 20 for shelling and winnowing, 10 for the second weeding, 10 for spreading NPK, 10 for treatment and bagging, and 20 for sowing. The labour is spread over the season rather than concentrated on one day. If you are asking whether 55 days on one hectare is feasible for a family with a budget, ICAT would be the place to ask, since the catalogue gives no cost and no yield gain.

The catalogue gives one example and does not say how many hectares it covers: a hectare in practice is larger than half, but its yield on that hectare varies, and the method is a choice of which practices fit your land. What it says is that in the south, around May-September, the main crop is usually grown with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and that the improved varieties it recommends are for shorter inter-planting intervals, such as 75 to 85 days for soya, cowpea or groundnut. Its brochure says the same thing in its own words: the idea is to run a succession of crops in the same plot. So half a hectare does not need it; it needs the method, and you need it to know whether the example it gives applies to your land. Ask ICAT.

per_item.reference: False on the brochure's own terms. It divides the country: in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops; in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is more often grown pure and it recommends running a succession instead of an association. So the same plan is not what it proposes. Beyond the region, it also asks you to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season before fixing a rotation, which is a plot by plot matter. For what suits your plot and your region, ICAT.

history.content: True or false: I can run the same plan anywhere in Togo.

draws.answer: False, but not because the plan is not good there. The five year development template is written for one hectare of Obatanpa, so a plan made for your field may have to be raised from 3 m by 3 m to 4 m by 4 m for Obatanpa itself, and there are proportions that scale with the area. What applies everywhere is the sequence: maize at the head of the rotation, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. And the two things that cost you more anywhere: tractor ploughing, and the NPK and urea. ICAT can show which of the five versions suits your plot.

False, and on the whole the brochure warns against it. The catalogue says each operation needs to be adapted to the region: the main plot is chosen in July, the plot chosen in April, the fertiliser is added at the stage specified by the soil check, and the tractor work is carried out during the rains. It does not say which regions it cannot be done in, and it does not put the answer anywhere. Ask ICAT or ITRA for a real answer in your own prefecture, and leave the rest to them.

per_item.reference: The spacing is not in what I hold. The ITRA and ICAT variety table gives, for each of the nine, the cycle, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, and it tells you to buy the seed only from approved sellers and to weigh the cycle and the yield when choosing. It does not give sowing distances, and those differ enough between varieties that guessing would cost you. Ask ICAT or ITRA, who are also the ones to tell you which variety suits your region this season and where the approved sellers are near you.

history.content: How far apart do I sow these varieties?

draws.answer: The spacing I can give you is the two marked spacing between varieties: 100 cm by 80 cm for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and 80 cm by 40 cm for Ikenne 18-24. The second variety, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, is marked 70 cm by 55 cm. And the brochure says to use a tolerant variety wherever possible, so it is a rule you can follow in other regions. Ask ICAT which of the two suits your region.

The spacing is the same for all, 80 cm by 40 cm, so you do not need to widen it, but which one is worth knowing, because the cycle and the spacing do differ. For the two main types, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 90 days for the first and 75 to 85 days for the second, so the spacing changes from 80 cm by 40 cm to 90 cm by 40 cm to 75 to 85 cm by 40 cm. For the improved varieties, there is no difference in the spacing, and you choose on their cycle and on the yield. ICAT will tell you which one suits your region this season.

per_item.reference: Two to four metres between the plants inside a row, and 10, 20 or 30 m between one row and the next, with the crop grown in the alley between. Lay the rows across the slope, never up and down it. The fertiliser trees named are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida. The crops named for the alleys are maize and cowpea. First pruning between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, with a high cut at 2 m above the ground advised.

history.content: ecartement arbres cultures en couloirs

draws.answer: Plant the arborial crops in a staggered pattern so the alleys are not straight lines. First, determine the spacing between plants: 2 to 4 m for the fast-growing varieties like soya, cowpea or groundnut, 10 to 20 m for the intermediate ones such as cowpea, groundnut or groundnut with legumes, or 100, 150 or 200 trees per hectare. Then set the rows 1 to 2 m apart in the row and 10, 20 or 30 m between the alleys. Build the alleys 1 to 1.5 m wide and use banco for the slow-growing species or gravel for the fast ones. Weed the plot at 15 to 25 days, then continue weeding and pruning from ~2 months on. For a planting schedule and the best variety for your area, go to ICAT.

In the dry savanna zone, set rows 1 to 2 m apart, which is 20 to 25 trees per pocket; in the bandova zone, put 1 m by 1 m, so 25 to 30 trees per pocket, giving 30 to 35 pockets; in Centrale, use the intermediate spacing of 2 m by 2 m. Plant during the rainy season. Use healthy seed setts, let the cut faces heal in shade and dust them with wood ash before sowing. Weed the field 2 to 3 times while the plants are small. For a tolerant striga-free variety, see ICAT or ITRA.

per_item.reference: Cut across it and you see a shape that is wide at the bottom and narrower at the top, with sloping sides. At ground level, the lower base measures 80 cm to 100 cm across. At the top, the upper base measures 35 to 40 cm, so it is roughly half the width of the foot, or less. Between the two, the height stands at 30 to 35 cm, so it comes up to about the middle of your shin. The earth in it is damp and packed, not loose, because the catalogue has you water it as you build it in order to compact it well. And along the run, towards each end, the wall is deliberately interrupted: those gaps are the spillways, provided to evacuate the excess water. A secondary bund is the same shape one size down: 70 to 80 cm at the foot, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high.

history.content: Describe a main bund to me as if I had cut through it.

draws.answer: You are looking at a water level, one of the six the catalogue names, and it is the one the catalogue recommends for building a main bund. It has two purposes: carrying water over the whole of the site so it is distributed properly over the whole of it, and holding the water so it runs along the sides rather than up and over the top. The difference you would see by cutting through it is that water is following the lines it was meant to follow, not the lines you draw around it. On a main bund it is 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high. On a secondary one it is 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30.

Cut across it; the water is moving up and down inside. Two separate things: the lower base, 80 to 100 cm across, which is 30 to 35 cm deep, and the upper base, 35 to 40 cm, which is 35 to 40 cm high. The main bund is built in layers, each watered as it is laid: the smaller ones go out first at 30 cm by 30 cm, 17 by 17 by 30, then 25 by 25 by 25, then 35 by 25 by 25, then 80 by 80 by 35. Each layer goes down to meet the one below it, which is why the bund rises rather than stands straight. Water it as you build, not after: the catalogue says to water them as you build so that they compact. And leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, which carry the excess water out.

per_item.reference: Choose an improved variety, and that is the control. Most of the improved varieties released in Togo are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the protection; AB11 is the one the table marks specifically as tolerant to streak, 90 to 100 days, 4 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3 on average, white grain. That is also an argument against sowing grain from your own granary, which the brochure warns against because it germinates badly, and against buying improved seed from anywhere but an approved seller. ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.

history.content: What do I do about maize streak?

draws.answer: The everyday name is maize streak. The disease is called stalk borer. While the plants are young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500 to 2,000 plants. Do not apply neem powder alone because the oil will burn the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in the same field. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

The everyday name is maize streak. Use a tolerant variety and, when you see streaks in leaves, apply an approved product at the label-specified rate. First, detect the streaks early, because the product will be used. Then wait to treat until you are sure the streaks are present, not after a rain or a disease outbreak. After applying the treatment, visit ICAT to get the current approved product and the correct dose.

per_item.reference: Then you are already partway through the cycle and the next year is settled. Groundnut is a legume, one of the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, which the catalogue puts in year one alongside beans and cowpea. So the year that follows it is maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot, sown now that the soil is rich in nitrogen. After that, year three is a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four is an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to the legumes. The brochure's version of the same idea reads maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, so if you prefer a fallow to the okra year, that is in the sources too. One plot is enough for all of it, since a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot. Take it to ICAT for what suits your region.

history.content: I have been told to rotate but nobody has told me what order.

There are two orders in the sources and they agree with each other. Tell me what the plot carried last season, because the catalogue says to take account of that and of the fertility of the soil before fixing anything.
Groundnut last season, and before that maize.

draws.answer: Then the order is right and the order is right at the same time. Groundnut is the one crop it puts the rotation to within a rotation: a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, and its rule is that the soil should be rotated, so it wants a soil that is not always cropped. Its position in the band around maize is at the head of the list, which means cereals, then legumes, then a root crop, then a fallow, so the order is maize then groundnut then maize then fallow. The brochure adds that a rotation improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of crops, so it wants a rotation that uses a legume as one of its four components, which is not lost in the list. What does not appear is what the brochure says about how to do it, since that is its own instruction rather than something to take out of the general rule. Take ICAT to work out which rotation suits your plot and your region.

Then the order you have is correct. The brochure says maize is a hungry plant that consumes a lot at panicle initiation, which is why it is followed by a legume, and it says the legume is a legume, that is a legume, a legume. And it says the maize after is a hungry plant that takes nutrients, so a hungry crop needs a hungry crop, so the order is maize then groundnut then maize. The rest of the table is the same rule: legumes named as improving plants, so cowpea, groundnut, soybean, with the option of striga tolerance in the case of soya. One more thing, since this is a rotation for a rotation: maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow.

per_item.reference: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least five compartments, well aired and roomy. One compartment with a shared yard for the breeders. One for brooding, where the eggs you collect and give back to the hens are hatched. One chick room. And two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. Beside the building, plan a grassy run for the birds and a store. Note this is the commercial model, not the banco henhouse of the family compound, which is smaller.

history.content: How should I build the henhouse for a commercial local hen unit?

draws.answer: Use banco for local breeds and cement bricks for improved breeds, always on a rammed or cemented floor you can clean and disinfect. The compartment is at least five compartments: a breeder section with fewer openings to limit heat, a chick room with fewer openings and an airy space, and an older hatching unit. Sweep the floor each day. Change the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months and disinfect each time you replace it. Provide enough feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes so the birds do not fight over them. For the exact dimensions for your flock, see ICAT.

Build the Improved Traditional Poultry House of birds at 3 by 3 metres, and give it at least five compartments: a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, 2 m high, and openings left for air; two of 1 m by 1 m for the breeders, one wall of 1 m high, 0.6 m by 0.5 m, and a roof that is raised with an inflow and outflow well. Sweep the inside of the henhouse daily. Change the litter of straw or rice husks every two to three months and disinfect each time you replace it. Add a yard for the birds to roam, and keep a fenced run towards the house so the chickens do not wander. The first health priority is a fenced run to keep the birds from wandering.

per_item.reference: No, and here anything is not better than nothing. You would build on it, the building would stand for twenty years, and neither of us would ever know whether the guess was right. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is detailed about this henhouse, the five compartments, the densities, the wall heights, the feeders and drinkers by age, the brooder, the manure pit, and it does not say which way the building faces. That silence is information: it tells you to ask someone who knows the ground rather than someone who has read the study. ICAT holds the plans and is the right place. I will give you anything in the reference without hesitation; this is not in it.

history.content: Just give me your best guess on the orientation, anything is better than nothing.

draws.answer: Nothing is better than nothing, and I would rather tell you that plainly than let you live with a guess. The catalogue gives the orientation without a reason, and a wrong answer costs you a season: north or south, that is the two things to know before fixing a curtain, before deciding what to do with the ground between. What it does not give is why, so I will not add a reason it does not have, and I will not suggest a reason on someone else's behalf. What it does give is the catalogue itself, with the two volumes of the layout, and the dimensions for the main bunds. ICAT for the direction, and ANAMET for the slopes.

I will not, because giving a guess is exactly what the instruction asks for. The catalogue starts with the orientation as the first step and describes how to read it, so a guess is reading against the source. I will also tell you what a guess would cost you: nothing. I will tell you what to do instead of guessing.

per_item.reference: That is exactly the condition this practice is aimed at. The aim the catalogue states is to build basins and drains so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. Begin where it begins, with measurement rather than with earth: determine the slopes with a water level, made from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and draw the plan from them. Then peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare and build, watering the bunds as you go so they compact, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund.

history.content: My rice drowns at one end and burns at the other in the same season.

draws.answer: The problem is waterlogged soil in your rice. Begin by opening shallow drainage channels so water can flow away from the plot instead of staying. After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn damage. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.

That is the main problem and the one the brochure gives for it. The catalogue says the rule is watered properly, that is as under-watered as well as over-watered, and that a water point is the better option than a bucket. So keep the water in the plan, and make sure it circulates well, which is why it names aeration as one of the things to do when there is a problem with too much water. If the end of the channel remains dry while the other one is soaking, that is a different issue and the answer is to water the dry section.

per_item.reference: False. The ratio both Togolese references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference builds its minimum commercial nucleus on it: 60 hens and 6 cocks. What sets how many chicks you get is the laying and the hatching, not the number of cocks. In that reference it is about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and six production cycles a year. Extra cocks fight, tread the hens bare and eat feed for nothing. Cull back to the ratio and put the effort into choosing the cock you keep, because he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.

history.content: True or false: more cocks means more chicks.

draws.answer: False. The ratio is one cock for about ten hens, which is a band that gives you two birds for every ten birds in the nucleus, not a rule that raises the hatching. A big number of cocks beats the number of chicks, and it is the same ratio every time you hatch and every time you raise up the young. What does not add up is the feeding: at six months a hen in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference eats 80 grams of feed a day, and at eight to ten weeks a cock eats 25 to 35 grams a day, so two cocks eating one would be taking more feed than they produce. The same reference says hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that is worth getting onto a little grassland if you can.

False. The ratios the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on are one cock for about ten hens, with that to the sale: a breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for that study, so about six hens per cock. The same reference works on about ten eggs per hen per laying and about six layings a year, which is why it sets down an annual projection of 5,500 eggs and a natural hatching rate near 70 percent. More cocks than that does not give more chicks: it gives more mature cocks and a better breeding dynamic than feeding poorly. Chicks are not sold.

per_item.reference: The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare is built on storing. Its profit depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, in 2005 evaluations, and the brochure says plainly that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. Storing well is what makes that possible: on treated pallets in an airy store the maize holds six months without weevil attack. Follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio before you fix the moment.

history.content: Sell straight after harvest or store first?

draws.answer: The catalogue advises against it and says what you are storing is the reason you are there. It says the brochure's own list is for maize kept long-term, and it is the store conditions in Maritime and Plateaux that make a stored maize acceptable. So the answer is not in the brochure's order but in its own words, and you should weigh what you are getting against the cost of keeping: a stored maize kept well will cost you less than one that has gone bad. I cannot tell you whether the store in your own field is good or not, so ask ICAT or ITRA.

Storing first matters, and the brochure puts it plainly: dry the grain well before selling. Sell after the grain has been dry, not after you have bought it. The storage instruction the brochure gives is a granary, with the maize protection set out: an airy type of rice straw, or a mixture of straw and wood shavings, sheltered from rain and wind; an approved insecticide, for a period of eight to ten days. And that is before you know what the buyer wants. Ask ICAT what is available near you and what is cheap.

per_item.reference: Count your hens and divide by ten. That is how many cocks to buy, because the ratio both references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and it is the same ratio that gives the commercial nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Then decide what you will look at in the market: vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and if you can, bought from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from whoever is at the stall, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. And have the quarantine ready before you leave the house: every newly bought bird goes two weeks apart from the flock, bought or given, so you do not bring a disease in.

history.content: I am about to buy cocks tomorrow. What do I work out tonight?

draws.answer: Work out how many cocks you need from your flock before the holiday, then plan the purchase. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so the number depends on your own flock. Start by setting a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, which is the commercial reference's band and gives you the ratio you work from: one cock for ten hens. Then count your eggs, set a gas incubator of 300 eggs on the flock, and decide the number of chicks to hat from them. Buy the cocks from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, and keep one for each ten hens. After that you hatch.

Count your birds in two ways before you buy. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a flock of 60 hens and 6 cocks, so two cocks is what you need for a unit of that size, and it should be counted from your own flock, not from the seller's promise. And decide whether you have the house where that count fits: the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for a henhouse of at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, and that is the compartment you are buying for. While you are waiting, look at the cocks again, because the ratio matters more than either way. Take the cocks out of the sale and into the count.

per_item.reference: I cannot name a breed for you, because neither Togolese reference names one. What they give is the ratio, one cock for about ten hens, and what to look for in the bird rather than in its breed: breeders taken from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds the weights you should see at six months, about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. For a named breed, and for where to buy it near you, ask ICAT. That is not something I should answer from memory.

history.content: Which breed of cock gives the best chicks?

draws.answer: The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists both the cocks from that study's own list, Tettah, Amen and Vezer, with the highest for hatching and survival: one cock for about ten hens. Its own six characteristics are vigorous and agile, a well developed bright red comb, a well developed bright yellow visodactylant, and a strong lean body. But in its own commercial model it names two more places for choosing: the one from the 2017 ESFT compendium, the 1.5 kg for 60 hens and 6 cocks, and the 3.5 kg for 60 hens and 12 cocks, which it adds are cheaper to keep and bring back more money. Whichever you pick, the 2020 reference's own work is the one to work it through.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not rank the breed, it says which to buy from and what to expect from whatever you choose. It is from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. What it does not do is tell you how many chicks to expect per hen, how long to keep them, how many to sell, or how to choose a keeper. Those are questions for ICAT or the animal health worker, and they are not something I can answer from here. What it does give you is the size you will need for your own flock: at one cock for about ten hens, the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Ask at the poultry market as well, because the 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing in its own words, in the choice of breeders.

per_item.reference: At least five, well aired and roomy. One compartment with a shared yard for the breeders; one for brooding, where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched; a chick room; and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. Beside the henhouse, plan a grassy run for the birds and a store. That is the commercial model of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The improved traditional henhouse of the family compound is a different building and does not take these dimensions.

history.content: combien de compartiments poulailler commercial

draws.answer: A commercial unit needs at least five. Two of them for the breeders, the age bands, 12 to 15 months for the chicks and 18 to 21 months for the growers. The one for the growers, 4 m by 3.5 m by 30 cm, that is 105 birds per square metre, and the chick room. And two of them for the drinkers, 2 m long by 1.5 m wide by 50 cm high for 50 birds, and one for the store.

At least five. One room with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room, and two run where the growers leave the farmers' ground. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sizes a commercial in all five on 8 m by 10 m, 50 birds each. It adds the ground you use for running the farm, and the manure pit well away from it. The building is also built to be disinfected at every change of litter, which is why it has to be opened and closed often.

per_item.reference: On a single line, 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, with the plants spaced 1 to 1.5 m apart. On a band of two or three lines, 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, with 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line. The curtain is planted against the dominant wind and oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side. Plant during the rainy season.

history.content: brise vent combien de plants par 100 m

draws.answer: A windbreak is planted in lines opposite the dominant wind, with trees placed 1 to 1.5 m apart, which gives 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. Place them opposite the wind so the wind passes through them, not through it. The windward side gets 66 plants, and the sheltered side gets 25 plants. Leave the ground around the windbreak clear of the weeds that would otherwise smother the plants. Plant during the rainy season.

The catalogue gives you the whole layout, not a number for each line, so I will not invent a number. It presents a windbreak as a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, with a windward side and a sheltered side, with a spacing of 1 to 1.5 m for the plants inside and 2 m between plants of the same species, with a low shrub layer at 10 to 20 cm, a taproot zone at 50 cm, and a canopy of 2 to 3 m at the lowest level. The dimensions are not in it. For which plants suit your ground and your climate, ICAT.

per_item.reference: One hard rain is not the settled rains. The maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and the sowing fiche says plainly not to sow on a first isolated shower. Check the window for where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, ask ANAMET what this season is doing before you follow your neighbours.

history.content: It rained hard once last week and everyone in the village is sowing.

draws.answer: Not in the south, where the rains run in one season. Maritime and Plateaux have two rainy seasons, April to May for sowing, and then June to July for the main crop. Kara and Savanes have one, May to June. Centrale sits between the two and behaves either way. So the first sowing is April in Maritime and Plateaux or June in Centrale, not January in the south. And widen your spacing in the second season, because maize is typically grown there after the first year. ICAT for your prefecture's calendar.

It is not what the calendar says, it is what it does not say. The maize brochure states that in the south, April and May are the two month windows for sowing, and that in Centrale, Kara and Savanes the rains are better one block at a time, so that sowing is not at the first shower but at the first rain that lasts near the sowing time. One rain in the south is sowing for one season, and one in the north is the first of two seasons; the sowing calendar is the first season band for both regions. What sowing means is to have the plot ready to sow as soon as the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and to avoid late sowing. If a long spell should happen, the brochure has you sow early in it, because a shortened season means a shorter window.

per_item.reference: You have moved from a two season region to a one season one, so your whole calendar shifts. In Maritime you sowed in April and May; where you are now, in the Savanes, sowing is in June and July, once the rains are settled. Choose your plot in April rather than January, clear it in April and May, and plough with the first rains in June and July. FAO GIEWS puts the northern rains around May to October. Ask ICAT for the calendar of your new prefecture.

history.content: I have just moved from Lome to Dapaong and I do not know when to start.

draws.answer: Two things to weigh. The maize brochure says the reason to sow at the amber stage is that the maize then goes into the cycle and finishes in time, and that the second half is the long week of ten days at the end of the season, so the choice of when is the choice of when to sow. And check the prefecture, since the list is different: maize is more often associated with July for its varieties, so a second half of October in Dapaong means it is late in the year. Ask ICAT what season is ahead of you.

The difference is more than one region. Lome is in the south, around October to April, so you are in the south zone, one rainy season. Dapaong is in the north, around May to October, so you are in the north zone. The north, including Dapaong, has one rainy season; the south, including Lomé, has two rainy seasons. So the calendar for your new farm is different, and you should take it to ICAT rather than to the extension service, which answers zone questions.

per_item.reference: About 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock at six months, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for commercial local hens, which adds that cocks of that weight are very active sexually. Use it as a check when you buy breeders, together with the look of the bird: a good frame, vigorous and agile, and for a cock a well developed and bright red comb. Take them from a well-followed farm or a research centre.

history.content: What weight should a good local hen and cock reach at six months?

draws.answer: A good local hen and cock both reach it at about 1.3 kg live weight at six months, so the difference is the cock by a little more. The cock is what decides the flock in the end, because the ratio is one cock for about ten hens, and it decides whether the chicks are well grown and agile. That is the ratio in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. Feed them apart from the chicks so they do not compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Give them clean water free-choice all day.

Both reach about 1.3 kg for hens and about 1.5 kg for cocks at six months, both weigh off at about 1.5 kg for hens and about 2 kg for cocks after a year of keeping. Both are cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists the cock as the one determining factor for a well followed flock. The same reference says to choose the breeder birds from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. Those figures come from the 2017 ESFT compendium.

per_item.reference: That is the wrong way round. A longer variety needs more days of rain, not fewer, so a late start makes it more likely to be caught at the end. The released list runs 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 90 to 95 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 90 to 100 for AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR, 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, 105 to 115 for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. A shortened season points to the short end. And whatever you sow, sow it when the rains are properly settled, not on one isolated shower. ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.

history.content: If the rains are late I should sow a longer variety to catch up.

draws.answer: Sowing a longer variety is not the same as catching up. The brochure puts the limiting factor as the short window: the main season is around May to October, so a crop needing more days in the season is sown at the start of it. A longer season needs a longer cycle, not a later date. What a longer season means is that you fix your sowing date for the longer end of the season and choose a variety that suits your region this season, which is where ICAT can help.

The brochure answers that exactly, and it gives a reason: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Its instruction is to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and to avoid an early sowing that would be done on a first shower. So the variety is not the thing, it is the timing. Check the season for your prefecture before you buy, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. ICAT for your prefecture, ANAMET for this year's rains.

per_item.reference: October falls in the second rains of the south: FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons there, around March to June and again around October. But none of the references I hold says which crop to sow in a given month, so I will not name one. What they do give is the main season calendar for Plateaux, sowing in April and May when the rains are settled, and that the second season plot in the south is chosen in July. For October in your own prefecture, ask ICAT, and ANAMET for this year's rains, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year.

history.content: What can I sow in the region of the Plateaux in October?

draws.answer: In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, the Plateaux region is where the rains come in two seasons, around March to June and again around October. FAO GIEWS describes the pattern as two rainy seasons, around March to June and again around October. The Centrale region has a single season, about May to September. Know your prefecture: in Maritime and Plateaux you wait for the first rains, around March to June, and sow when they are established, around April to May; in Centrale you are in the centre and need to wait for the second season. Sow early enough, since the second season is short. Ask ANAMET for this year's onset and ACRL for the calendar.

The Plateaux area is for maize two to three months after sowing and the plot is cleared and prepared in April and May, or June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The plot is chosen in July. In October the plot is not chosen, so the rule for October is not a rule for October: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower. What you need to wait for is that the season has settled, and the plot is cleared and ready.

per_item.reference: You are running one cycle where the model runs six. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, which is why it asks for at least five compartments: a breeder compartment, a brooding compartment, a chick room and two grower compartments, all occupied at once by birds of different ages. Start staggering: set a batch of eggs, then another before the first leaves the brooder at three weeks, and so on. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs, and the brooder is meant to handle small hatchings in series, so the equipment already assumes this. Staggering also spreads your sales, which matters because you are meant to find buyers before each batch is ready. Write the settings and hatchings in the movement register so you can see the rhythm build.

history.content: Everything on my farm is the same age and the henhouse is empty half the year.

draws.answer: Then two things are wrong and I will name them. Counting by eye is cheap enough for a small area, so a full hundred birds at one age is a real number, not a band. Work in the ratio rather than in the age: 60 hens and 6 cocks, one cock for ten hens in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so you are near it but with two things to check. If the cocks died together with the birds you are not in the proper ratio, and if you have bought birds from anywhere other than a well followed farm or a research centre, then the age is off. And check the movements, which are what the reference wants you to keep track of: sales, hatchings and deaths, so if culls, hatchings and deaths are not balanced, the age falls past the ratio. Follow through with the culls and the hatchings, and ask ICAT if anything is missing.

The two things that do not move are the age of the birds and the movement of the hens. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, with the same proportions of breeders, brooders and growers. It also counts the movements: the sales, the hatchings and the deaths, with the culled birds thrown out. So the ages do not follow the same pattern. What does follow is the management: the flock must be renewed at least twice a year, with the cockerels born on the farm. If yours stays quiet, look at the movements first.

per_item.reference: False. A hen in lay takes 80 grams a day in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, while a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes 25 to 35 grams a day, and one from 1 to 60 days takes 10 to 25 grams a day. The laying hen is the biggest eater of the three, and she also takes the most mineral: 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, where the younger bands take 3 kg. Over a whole period the growers add up to about 5 kg a bird from 61 days to sale, and about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days.

history.content: True or false: a growing bird eats more than a laying hen.

draws.answer: False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts four, and each is sized for a different role: about 1.5 kg a day from 1 to 60 days, about 5 kg a day from 61 days to sale at six months, and about 10 kg a day for a hen in lay. So a bird in the breeding band takes the most, and a bird in the grower band takes the least. The layens take the most feed as well, 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed.

False. The reference gives a laying hen about 80 grams a day in all, about 10 to 25 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months, and a hen in lay takes far more than that, 80 grams a day across the entire period of her life. The chicks are fed differently: 10 to 25 grams a day, and about 5 to 10 grams a day from 1 to 60 days. So the difference is seen at the end of the year.

per_item.reference: Halve the formula for 100 kg. The 2020 ICAT and PASA laying formula is 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg, so for 50 kg take 28.75 kg of cereals, 5 kg of cake, 5 kg of fish meal, 7.5 kg of bran and 3.75 kg of mineral mix. Make the mineral mix from 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of calcined bone, 2 kg of charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt per 10 kg.

history.content: I want to mix 50 kg of laying feed. What quantities?

draws.answer: You need about 62.5 kg of mineral mix and 57.5 kg of water for 50 kg of laying feed, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. Split those quantities: 62.5 kg of oyster or snail shell, 10 kg of crushed calcined bone, 10 kg of crushed charcoal and 2.5 kg of kitchen salt for the minerals; 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Make the water freely available at all times.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 57.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed for 100 kg of laying, and 10 kg of cake for the youngest birds. So for 50 kg of laying you need about 14.75 kg of the mix and 5 kg of cake. Make sure the free extras fit too, which are greenery, termites and maggots, and don't forget the mineral mix itself: 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt.

per_item.reference: No, the rule holds at any number: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. What half a flock changes is the urgency of everything around treatment. When disease shows up in the flock the reference gives six things to do: isolate the sick birds; forbid any trading in your henhouse; forbid any visit without a precise purpose; inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly; never eat the carcasses; and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Do those now rather than shopping for medicine, and let the veterinary service name what you are dealing with.

history.content: Half my flock is sick. Does that change what treatment can do?

draws.answer: Yes, and it is worth knowing before you buy anything, because a guess costs you a bird and a flock. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks is a quarantine, separate the sick birds from the healthy ones, and neither of those is cheap: a quarantine is two weeks for every bird that arrived on someone else's henhouse. Do not eat the carcasses for a moment; burn them or bury them and bury the soil.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not treat partial sickness as a separate issue, so treating half is treating the same animal twice. What it says is that if you isolate the sick birds, take them out, and forbid any trading in your henhouse, the disease is not caught by movement. What it does not do is give you a double answer on treatment or dose. For a second infection, call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, and bring the dead birds out with a burning procedure.

Then TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, because the brochure counts both on the cycle and on the tolerance, and both are marked striga tolerant. per_item.reference: It is the size the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference pairs with sixty breeding hens, so it is not too big as equipment. But the reference itself flags the economics: at that flock size the keeper should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. So plan the hatching service alongside your own eggs. Remember also that the natural way exists: a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs, and incubation takes twenty-one days either way.

history.content: Is a 300-egg incubator not too big for sixty hens? Justify.

draws.answer: The 300 eggs per hen in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is a single number and the machine is a machine, not a measure of how many hens it will cover. If sixty hens are sitting in one room, they are all on the machine at the same time, which is the reference's business. The reference does not say whether you can spread it over several machines, so I have no figure to give you. What I can tell you is what the reference does give: at that size you hatch for other keepers as well, and it is worth asking.

The 300 egg incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of sixty breeding hens. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference size a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of sixty breeding hens, and it says that reference's size is the minimum that gives a reasonable hatching. It also tells you that if you hatch more than one bird per egg at all, you should hatch less, which is the same point: a gas machine of that size is the minimum efficient unit for sixty eggs. So yes, a 300-egg machine suits sixty hens and lets you stay within the reference's own range.

per_item.reference: Eighty grams a day for a hen in lay, which is the figure the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives and the highest of its age bands. For comparison, a bird from 1 to 60 days eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day, and from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing as one range, between 5 and 90 grams a bird depending on age and size. A laying hen also takes the most mineral of any band: 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, against 3 kg for the younger birds.

history.content: My hens are laying and I do not know how much to put out each day.

draws.answer: I cannot tell you how much to feed because the figures in the references are per hundred birds and the daily limit changes with age. Use the ration as a template: 10 kg of cereals, 2.5 kg of cake, 2 kg of fish meal, 2 kg of bran and 0.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed. The laying hen takes the most mineral of all, about 7.5 kg. For the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference the lay formula is 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg. Ask ICAT where to buy cakes and mineral mix.

per_item.reference: You already have the habit the poultry sheet asks for. It says to sweep the inside of the house two or three times a week and to throw the droppings into a manure pit away from the house, and it adds that those droppings can serve to fertilise the fields. The 2020 catalogue picks the same thread up on the agroforestry side, where it lists using animal droppings and plant debris for composting among the ways a grower raises income. The compost sheet shows where they sit in the heap: after the base of slow rotting material comes a layer of manure 5 cm thick, then about 30 cm of plant residues on top, trodden down. One thing I should be exact about. Neither document tells you in so many words to empty your pit into your heap. Putting the three together is a step you can take, not a sentence I am quoting. Either way, keep the pit away from the house, and keep the heap in the shade, sheltered from wind and rain.

history.content: I sweep my poultry house two or three times a week and the droppings are piling up behind it. What do I do with them?

draws.answer: You should sweep the floor of your poultry house each time the birds go to bed, then mix the droppings with the soil and use them to make compost as often as you can, for example every 2-3 months, and bury the residues deep in the heap. Keep the litter that is wet, dirty or diseased, and spray disinfectant inside the shelter. Make sure the house is located near a clean water point and a manure pit is close to it. An extension officer can teach you the proper rooster and the correct way to feed.

The droppings have to be collected and then burned or buried so they do not rot and produce gas. First, gather the droppings into a manure pit. Build it at least 1.5 m by 2 m by placing the walls to the side so the house does not get wet. Dig a shallow drainage channel around the house to let rain run off. Place the pit well away from the house. Sweep the inside of the house two or three times a week and turn the droppings into the pit. The first step also applies to the litter: sweep it on top of the droppings every two to three months.
